@@136788981 <h> How power from the people carbon-dates the opposition <p> We were told that it was impossible , insane even , to attempt . But it 's actually working . In a world of woe , Australia can be quietly pleased with progress on an important reform . <p> The electricity grid is moving towards renewables at a rate faster than experts predicted . For two quarters in a row now , solar and wind have supplied about half of the nation 's electricity . Coal 's share is shrinking to all-time lows . <p> Illustration by Simon Letch <p> The grid has remained stable . The price of wholesale electricity has come down . Carbon emissions have fallen . And the price of a lamb roast is yet to hit $100 . Far from it . <p> Is this because demand for electricity has fallen ? On the contrary , demand has reached record highs , thanks to heatwaves . <p> Advertisement <p> " Not long ago , that would have sent energy ministers out to ask people to not turn on their dishwashers , " says federal Energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ coped fine . This is a turning point . " <p> What 's going on ? Like Hemingway 's famous description of how bankruptcy happens , the electricity transition has proceeded " gradually , then suddenly " . <p> " The story is that there 's a big shift to a lot more battery storage , and that 's changing the market in interesting ways , " says Grattan Institute energy and climate change program director Alison Reeve . " All the batteries are starting to mop up daytime solar energy and then people are using it at the evening peak . That 's flattening demand peaks . If it continues , it 's a great sign . " <p> How so ? <p> " The lower you make your peak , the smaller the overall grid needs to be , " Reeve says . " And that saves everyone a lot of money . " <p> Advertisement <p> Another change : " We used to have gas peakers turning on at 5pm , " she says , referring to the gas-fired power plants that switch on to supply the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " That 's very expensive . " But the surge in new batteries is making gas peakers redundant and that cuts the cost . <h> Related Article <p> " The story of the last 20 years has been coal leaving the grid . Now we are starting to see gas leaving the grid , " Reeve says . <p> That does n't make gas obsolete . Heavy industry depends on gas , and 5 million homes use it too . But it does make it a little less central ; we have a glimpse of the future . Better yet , the change is giving Australia 's electricity market some insulation from the world energy crisis . <p> The last time there was a global oil shock was in 2022 , when Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine . Oil prices leapt by about 60 per cent . The Australian wholesale electricity price leapt yet higher in response , by some 200 per cent . But this time , while the global price is up by about 70 per cent due to the Iran war , Australia 's wholesale electricity price remained @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ firm Wood Mackenzie . <p> Advertisement <p> In fact , wholesale power in Australia is cheaper now than it was in January , before the war broke out . The bottom line : " The country 's power sector is steadily decoupling from global fossil fuel market volatility , " says Wood Mackenzie analyst Natalie Thompson . <p> In the midst of a fuel crisis , this is very welcome news . Perhaps not for some Coalition politicians who 've staked their careers on opposing the shift to renewables , however . <p> Australia has expanded its renewables to the point that they supplied the majority -- 51 per cent -- of electricity in the last quarter of last year . It was the first time . In Western Australia , which operates separately , the comparable statistic was even higher , at 52.4 per cent renewables . <p> Of all the batteries being installed worldwide today , one in 10 is in Australia . <p> The Coalition , allergic to electoral majorities , intensified its phobia to electric majorities in exactly the same quarter . Renewable energy " has all been a scam " and Australians had been " brainwashed " , the One Nation leader says . If so , it 's been effective . Renewables are partly a people 's movement . Families have led installations of solar panels for decades now . The total number of households with rooftop systems is 4.3 million . That 's rapidly approaching half the country . <h> Related Article <p> Altogether , the capacity of the people 's panels movement " now exceeds the total capacity of existing coal-fired power plants " , Wood Mackenzie reports . <p> And the battery boom is partly a people 's movement . In the eight years since , Australia has hooked up batteries with a combined capacity 45 times this size . In the last year alone , the installed capacity of batteries , home-scale and grid-scale , in Australia has more than doubled . Of all the batteries being installed worldwide today , one in 10 is in Australia . <p> Donald Trump 's war has galvanised a boom in EV demand in Australia , too . @@136789479 <p> Our continent by continent expert update showcasing what 's hot and what 's not right across the world . See all stories . <p> With bookings on the rise , Africa is one of the most aspirational destinations . No longer just a " one day " vision board dream , the continent is enjoying a surge in Australian visitors . From the jungles of Rwanda to the ancient " Louvre of the Desert " , this extraordinary continent is finally calling us home . <h> THE LOWDOWN <p> Africa is big -- bigger by far than it appears on most maps . This misrepresentation is the fault of the Mercator projection , a commonly used template developed by 16th century Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator , which supersizes some regions ( we 're looking at you , Greenland ) while shrinking the very cradle of humankind . Do n't be fooled by these " imperial " measurements : this behemoth of a continent accommodates a mind-boggling assortment of languages and ethnicities and a hefty share of topographical diversity . These ingredients are key to the travel trends identified by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cultural immersion , heritage storytelling and conservation-led experiences . With bookings on the rise , according to a 2026 trends report by tour operator Collette , Africa is one of the most aspirational destinations . <p> " Africa has always held a sense of awe and mystery , " says Collette director Roger Clulow . " For many travellers it 's a bucket-list destination and somewhere that they were never really sure they 'd ever get to visit . " <p> Cost has been an obstacle but rising prices elsewhere have levelled the " paying " field , according to Marco Rosa , co-founder of luxury boutique hotel specialist Plateau International . " In the past , Africa used to be much more expensive than other places , so you needed to set a higher budget . Now , it 's not because the cost of travel to Africa has gone down , it 's because all the other destinations have increased in price . So for Australians travelling to Africa , it 's levelling up . " <p> Reason enough , for those still dilly-dallying , to cast off @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ WHAT 'S HOT <p> Ethiopia is on the ( literal ) radar , with Ethiopian Airlines announcing plans to launch direct flights to Australia in 2028 pending the acquisition of suitable aircraft ; two undisclosed Australian destination cities have been shortlisted and a new airport , expected to be Africa 's biggest when it opens in 2030 , is also under construction 45 kilometres from the capital , Addis Ababa . Adventure travel is sizzling , and South Africa is one of the best places to hike , abseil and shipwreck-dive . Relaxation is also hot : last year nearly 1 million international visitors arrived in the Tanzanian archipelago of Zanzibar , an idyllic post-safari bolt-hole . <h> WHAT 'S NOT <p> Let 's address the elephant in the room : safety . @@136819210 <h> ANALYSIS : The cuts to the NDIS that will be confirmed in the budget force the disabled community to pay the price of systemic abuse and neglect . By Georgia Cranko . <h> The personal politics of the NDIS <p> Rigorously stress-cleaning the kitchen felt like the most sensible thing to do while I listened to Health Minister Mark Butler announce the latest round of National Disability Insurance Scheme reforms , because I needed something to focus on when everything else felt uncertain . It turned out he was doing something similar at a national scale : tidying , sorting , scraping , reclassifying , trying to turn a complex system that caters to complex lives into something that could seem tidy and simple . <p> The difference is that when government cleans up the NDIS , it is not scraping away clutter or sticky residue where it should not be . It 's stripping back the hope that drove the scheme when it was established , the understanding that social and community participation is a civil right rather than something to be measured or justified repeatedly . At @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ day I could live in a society that takes collective responsibility for each other 's wellbeing . <p> That hope did not come from government , it came from people who were excluded from community altogether . People placed in institutions , group homes , segregated schooling , or systems where you were not expected to speak , not expected to decide , often not told you ever had a voice to begin with -- so the idea that your life could be political , that your experience was important enough to listen to , had to be cultivated and defiantly claimed . Those people fought for decades to deinstitutionalise , and for social recognition . It is humbling to think my life now is possible because of that legacy . <p> I remember being about 20 , standing at a rally and hearing politicians argue for the NDIS while referring to disabled people as citizens who deserved much more -- and not as a burden , or children in depleted families or perpetual drains on burnt-out carers . It was the first time I had heard that said publicly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and it actually made me cry , and still does . My emotional response to being considered in broader social policy still takes me off guard , because it should be a social baseline . I live in the same culture and have largely accepted how easily disability is treated as a niche issue that draws charity more readily than respect . <p> As the NDIS was written into policy , I started to understand that access to community , work , education and ordinary life was not an extra . It was part of what a social welfare system existed to fund , and I did not always have to compromise and prove I was worthy of support . <p> Disability activist Stella Young often quoted a line from another activist , Laura Hershey : " You get proud by practising . " <p> In honour of them both , I now have that line tattooed on my right biceps , because pride is not something that ever gets nurtured . It is vital to keep insisting you matter , through prioritising access , through repetition , through being @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ When the world you are born into constantly denies you are enough of a person to cater for , pride becomes harder to sustain , so practising is needed . For many years , I did not see the point of having pride about who and what I am . <p> That is why the sentiment of the personal being political is so central to how I live , and I feel it is for many other disabled people . Any act of ordinariness , of claiming space , or taking care of ourselves and those around us , is resisting the burden narrative as a disabled person . It is too easy to succumb . There is no visible community to recognise yourself in , because people have been separated , contained , or placed into charitable systems that are prone to normalising neglect and abuse -- as though those affronts were individual experiences , not systemic failing . <p> Spending on social and community participation is being reduced and capped , singled out as a pressure point , even though it is the part that lets you leave @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that resembles an ordinary life . <p> The NDIS came from people refusing the idea that disability is something society accommodates when it is convenient , and insisting that exclusion is structural and therefore changeable . <p> So when Butler says the NDIS is " one of Australia 's great human rights achievements " , a part of me still hears the original social promise of leaving no one behind , that disability communities matter . <p> And then I hear what has actually been announced . <p> The scheme is being pulled back from a projected cost of more than $70 billion to about $55 billion by 2030 . It is called sustainability but feels like less room , less time , less capacity for lives like mine to exist inside it . Some 760,000 people are currently in the scheme , and that number is being reset closer to 600,000 , which means more than 160,000 people will not have NDIS support , even if nothing about their lives has changed . <p> Growth is being cut from about 10 per cent a year to about 2 per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where I am standing . I feel the ceiling being lowered while people are still trying to stand up under it . <p> Access is shifting away from diagnosis towards standardised functional capacity assessments . I already know what it feels like to translate a life into something measurable , to fit complexity into a framework that decides what counts and what does not , and how that framework becomes the human need that is legitimised . <p> I keep coming back to participation , because that is where I feel it most directly . Spending on social and community participation is being reduced and capped , singled out as a pressure point , even though it is the part that lets you leave the house , maintain relationships and hold onto something that resembles an ordinary life . <p> There have been countless investigations into abuse and neglect , accounts of supported housing bought up by investors who never deliver what is promised , of untrained security companies moving into behaviour management , and of people being trafficked and scammed by those who see disability support as a business @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ attention fades , as if the problems were due to isolated misuses of power and opportunistic " bad " people rather than to the lack of government oversight making it all possible . <p> The disability royal commission looked at this for years . It heard from thousands of people and documented violence , abuse , neglect and exploitation across homes , schools , workplaces and services -- not as isolated failures but as patterns produced by systems that were meant to support people . It ended with 222 recommendations calling for structural change so people with disability could live with dignity and full participation . <p> None of that is historical in the way people want to believe it is . <p> And still , Butler describes cases of abuse and neglect and then uses them to justify cutting support . As if the scandal were that disabled people had so much access to support that they were hampering adequate regulation . We do n't want to see that government actually grew the market , underfunded all that existed outside the scheme , failed to regulate it and then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> In his National Press Club speech last week , when Butler declared a commitment to " Nothing about us , without us " , I wondered if he has read the book where that rallying cry became embedded in disability rights history . Activist James Charlton wrote in 1998 that the phrase is " not a plea for pity " because disabled people " have had enough of that " . He then explained that hoping for adequate support " is useful only when it is not illusory , and help is useful only when it leads to empowerment " . That should be a hammer that hits you over the head . Participation and self-determination are not luxuries , not something to be scaled back , or overlooked when they become inconvenient . <p> I get angry when " Nothing about us , without us " is used as a flippant virtue signal , delivered after decisions have been made . Minister , that 's not how it works . Consultation should happen before reducing access , before deciding whose needs are sanctioned and how much of a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ calling this gaslighting is a stretch . @@136819217 <h> ANALYSIS : The coming budget provides an opportunity to make tax reforms that help keep the nation afloat during the present crisis , while providing equity and balance for future generations . By Dr Aruna Sathanapally . <h> The budget 's clashing priorities <p> In 2008 , when the global financial crisis hit , Australia 's response was swift . The federal government deployed a stimulus program amounting to more than $50 billion , or about 5 per cent of gross domestic product . It was one of the largest discretionary fiscal responses of any advanced economy . <p> Twelve years later , the Covid-19 pandemic forced the closure of large sections of the economy . Australia 's total discretionary fiscal response exceeded $360 billion , about 18 per cent of GDP . It was one of the largest economic interventions in Australia 's history . <p> It is often said that in Australia , we are good at crises . Certainly in both of these recent events we went hard early , and Australia managed to hold up its economy and living standards better than many of its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of us during the pandemic without turning on each other . <p> Australians look to government in a crisis , and survey data shows our trust in government lifts when we see action . <p> The reasons for our relative economic good fortune through both the GFC and the pandemic go beyond simply fiscal firepower , but acting to keep a floor underneath the Australian population is an imperative that any government faces when a crisis hits . <p> To date , this has involved having money to throw at the problem . History has shown that this spending is slow to unwind . In part , this is because crises provide the cover for other pent-up spending requirements finally to be addressed , without the hard conversation about raising revenue or finding savings to do so . When a shock looms , the surge to meet the moment has too often involved deprioritising , or dropping entirely , progress on Australia 's longer-term needs . Government -- and public -- bandwidth is limited , and a crisis eats it up . <p> The war in Iran and effective closure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a sustained shock to the global economy and possible recession . <p> To date , the government has done as well as could be expected to shore up fuel supplies from our trading partners . But it can not conjure up supplies if our trading partners start to run dry . <p> " In this budget , our government should trust in our better angels and do its best by younger Australians who are inheriting a harder , more expensive world . " <p> Treasury is preparing a downside scenario as part of the upcoming budget . It must . The war 's impact is like a rock rolling down a hill towards us : we will be hit but how hard is as yet unknown . Consumer price inflation has already risen , to 4.6 per cent in March from 3.7 per cent the previous month . <p> Regardless of the cause , Australians have come to expect governments to soften the blow of rising prices . This pressure has already resulted in fuel excise relief and free public transport in Victoria and Tasmania . Both are broad , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Conventional wisdom asks governments to be timely , targeted and temporary in their response to shocks . The International Monetary Fund has warned against untargeted energy subsidies or measures that distort price signals which guide consumers away from something in short supply . We will have to change our patterns of fuel consumption and this will have knock-on effects for prices and for livelihoods across the economy . <p> How the government can cushion this cost-of-living shock in the near term without worsening inflation is a genuinely difficult question , made more so by uncertainty over how the war will play out . A playbook for crisis response built on putting cash into all households will not work . And we now face a future of rolling shocks , running the gamut from armed conflict to extreme weather to technological disruption . <p> This budget is not an easy one . But we can not wait for this unpredictable event to pass before we get back to thinking about our known long-term challenges . <p> This is where the imperative to respond to the impacts of the war collides with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of months ago . This was meant to be the budget that rejected short-termism to start to adapt a tax system that is not match-fit for the future we face . <p> Last year 's post-election Economic Reform Roundtable laid the foundation for a broader economic reform agenda under the Albanese government . " Productivity-enhancing " measures were presented , many of which related to the slow grind of boosting Australia 's economic dynamism : harmonising regulation and occupational licensing to get to a single , national economy , and getting our cities to function like vibrant economic engines , rather than flinging workers to the fringes . Australia 's federal division of powers means that such reforms take sustained work , and sometimes money , to grease the wheels of jurisdictional cooperation . <p> On the final day of the round table , the door was opened to the possibility of long-neglected tax reform . <p> Opening those tax deliberations , I said that our national conversation needs to be about how we sustain a high-quality life for young people today and those who come after them , given @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> There is a set of measures firmly in the federal government 's hands . And this budget is a critical opportunity for the government to stand up to noisy losers and fix a tax and transfer system that has favoured older , wealthier Australians , and those who draw down our natural resources -- most notably gas -- in ways that are neither sustainable nor fair . <p> We are a relatively low-tax country , yet we have high service expectations and a large Boomer cohort moving into old age , stretching our health and care systems . <p> While Australia 's taxation of personal income is n't particularly onerous , the way we collect it is imbalanced . We lean most heavily on wages and salaries from work , while having very generous concessions for income from wealth and housing speculation and ways to manipulate tax through deductions and trusts . Redesigning taxation of fossil fuel exports and introducing a price on carbon emissions would give us revenue sources that go with the grain of the transition we need to make away from fossil fuels . <p> Finally , we can increase the GST . Taxing consumption is a less economically damaging way to raise necessary revenue , so long as we fully compensate poorer households . <p> These reforms remain wise even in the face of supply shocks . Reducing the preferential treatment of passive income will help us deal with one driver of persistent inflationary pressure in the economy : the continued growth in spending by wealthy older Australians , insulated from the Reserve Bank 's attempts to cool consumer spending . <p> The changes occurring to the world around us are stark . Rather , we need to crack on and tackle the longstanding problems we know how to solve . We need to rebalance the tax system , double down on the shift away from fossil fuels to electrification , and build more renewables , because our security depends on it . We need to invest in human capital , resilience and innovation , and encourage households and the private sector to do the same . @@136819232 <h> Novelist Robbie Arnott writes about the realities of the non-human world in ways that grant them meanings separate from the human . By James Bradley . <h> Writer Robbie Arnott 's rebellious path to real stories <p> Robbie Arnott 's books slip past the real into a world of primal wonder , yet he is wary of thinking too much about intentions or philosophy . He describes his writing in more intuitive terms , talking about sensibility , atmosphere , the ways history is written into the landscape . " It 's like there 's this amorphous feeling I 'm trying to give shape to , " he says . " And what I 've got to do is find the words and the rhythms that will get me there . " <p> When I speak to Arnott , who will be appearing at the Sydney Writers ' Festival this month , he is at home in the house in West Hobart that he shares with his lawyer wife , Emily , and their two young children . I had been worried about interrupting his writing time , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ frazzled , courtesy of a long day of domestic interruptions . <p> It 's oddly reassuring to find Arnott grappling with such quotidian problems . At only 36 , he has established himself as one of Australia 's most successful writers . Across four novels -- Flames , The Rain Heron , Limberlost and Dusk -- he has garnered critical praise , awards and an enthusiastic readership -- not things that always go together . <p> Arnott says he never had " a lightning bolt moment where I decided to be a writer . Nor did I have any tremendous trauma or pain that I needed to get down on the page " . His writing evolved out of his love of reading . Growing up in Launceston , he shared a room with his sister . Because she was two years older , she was allowed to stay up later if she was reading a book . " It was kind of a masterstroke by my parents , " he says . " A child 's sense of injustice could power whole suburbs . So I forced myself to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more . " <p> He became an obsessive reader , consuming industrial quantities of fantasy . When he was 13 his mother gave him a copy of Slaughterhouse-Five . " I was very sceptical because it was n't a cool fun book about explosions or swords , but it just blew my mind . It was like someone had put a crowbar inside my chest and cracked me open . I did n't realise books could do that to you . " <p> After Slaughterhouse-Five , Arnott began working his way through his parents ' bookshelves , mainlining literary novels in the same way he had fantasy . At 16 , he did work experience in the now-defunct Launceston branch of Fullers Bookshop . Later , he chose a place at the University of Tasmania rather than in Melbourne , because he knew he could get work at Fullers in Hobart . <p> At the bookshop he worked with Adam Ouston and Ben Walter . Both are now successful writers : Ouston 's first novel , Waypoints , was longlisted for the Miles Franklin , and Walter is the author @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ then , neither was published . <p> " Adam was lead singer of a very popular indie band in Hobart and was very cool , and Ben was this very whimsical poet , " says Arnott . " I 'd study English at university during the week and then come to work with them on the weekends . And Adam would ask me whether I 'd ever read Raymond Carver . I 'd never heard of Raymond Carver . So suddenly all the collections would come flying across the shop towards me . " <p> Meanwhile , the former owner of Fullers , Clive Tilsley , was pressing books by Tobias Wolff and others on him . This " dual education " rewired his brain , igniting a passion for American minimalism . " It also kind of cursed me because I tried to write like that for seven or eight years , " he says . " But I was n't very good at it . " <p> With the benefit of hindsight , Arnott can see the problem was cultural rather than technical . " There 's an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't work in an antipodean context . " His fascination with that mode has never really gone away . " The other day while I was doing the dishes I listened to somebody on The New Yorker podcast reading ' Elephant ' by Carver and I was reminded of just how brilliant he is and how out of reach that voice and style is to me . I 've published four novels now and it feels even further away than anything I could do . But it 's very , very seductive . " <p> His breakthrough came out of a moment of failure . " There was this whole idea in the University of Tasmania 's English department that Tasmania has its own island literature that 's different to everywhere else , " says Arnott . " And because I was young and obnoxious I really rebelled against that idea . I thought we should all be writing dirty realism . I moved to Melbourne for a job and tried to write like Helen Garner or Raymond Carver and it all went terribly wrong and I moved back to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a reading at a bookshop . " <p> " There 's a streak of late-in-life rebelliousness that 's emerged as an adult , that means I do n't want to do anything anyone expects me to do . " I decided to write something about where I 'm from but in a way that I 'd actually want to read ... And I thought , ' Well , I do n't actually know about anything . Written in a raw , elemental prose and leaping effortlessly between multiple perspectives , it transforms Tasmania into a magical landscape of signs and wonders . While it is , as Arnott acknowledges , " shaggy " , its pages also hum with a sense of possibility and discovery . <p> This sense of discovery remains central to Arnott 's process . His process is instinctive and exploratory , the shape and structure of his stories uncovered through the process of the writing rather than plotted out in advance . " If I knew @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , laughing , " I 'd be too bored to write the book . " <p> Arnott works sentence by sentence , allowing their rhythms to guide him . " I work hard on trying to describe things physically but also on trying to capture an emotional landscape , the movements and speech and patterns of characters and how that reveals things about them . " <p> This intuitive approach underpins his attitude to his work more generally . He believes readers can tell when a writer has written the book they think @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ write . " People seem to think that while you should stick close to major events , you can invent all sorts of small events around them . @@136819234 <h> Incidental Architecture keeps it simple in the Blue Mountains <p> When an architect describes a project as " dear to their heart " , it 's usually worth paying attention . The Sydney-based small practice Incidental Architecture says this of Gingkin , an off-grid house named for its location on a remote site west of the Blue Mountains . According to co-director Matt Elkan , " it exemplifies an awful lot for us " . <p> It also seems to exemplify the spirit of the moment . Who 's not dreaming of escape right now , slipping the bonds of the city and the news cycle to retreat to a solitary house , small and self-contained , on some lofty , cold plateau , to find solace away from the teeming frenzy ? <p> Gingkin sits on the edge between Gundungurra and Wiradjuri Country . Its elevation is about 1300 metres -- similar to Thredbo Village . The house follows all the articles of passive environmental design -- orientation maximising sun access to the north , thermal mass where it counts , careful siting with regard to prevailing winds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Paul Pholeros , who advised his students that in assessing a site , you should locate the house wherever you would put up your tent if you were camping . In this case , it meant ducking below the brow of a ridge for protection from the frigid westerlies and siting the house near a fringe of trees , facing outwards and upwards . The point , say the architects , is to be " in a big landscape , under a huge sky , with less stuff " . <p> The house has ample rainwater storage and an array of photovoltaic panels and batteries . It 's heated via hydronic radiators connected with a geothermal system . There 's no air-conditioning , but it opens up for cross-ventilation on the warmer summer days , while a highly insulated , high-performance building envelope keeps out the cold . <p> The plan is almost Palladian in its discipline and organisation : an orderly square formed by a rigorous construction grid , creating a series of small cellular rooms that can be closed off for efficient heating . It 's not built @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ model before , notably in the Kazahana lodge built in the very snowy Nagano Prefecture in Japan . At Gingkin the approach is less technical and for all the language of building science -- a heat pump with a coefficient of performance of six ! Double low-E glazing ! -- the architects are anxious to avoid what they describe as a " sustainability by checklist " approach . Sustainability , they say , is logic . <p> It may not be super fancy , but it 's exceptionally precisely assembled : tight as a drum and crisp as a new apple . <p> Incidental Architecture has a long association with the Alternative Technology Association , an advocacy and resource group for sustainable housing now known as Renew , and the architects cite the idea that in a low-energy house you do n't necessarily need to be comfortable in all of the rooms all of the time , only in some of them all of the time . At Gingkin the smaller , cosy spaces are pushed to the edges towards the light , leaving a higher central space with a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ northern sun to the centre of the plan . Outdoor suntrap decks are tucked into the volume on each side -- a place out of the wind -- and catch the first or last light of the day . <p> The building was economical by the standards of bespoke architect-designed houses , with a square-metre build rate of $4800 per square metre internally and $2400 for the covered outdoor decks . The architects ascribe this to efficient use of materials and bog-standard , lightweight construction techniques . @@136819237 <h> Justine E. Hausheer The Vanishing Wild <p> In The Vanishing Wild : Australian wildlife and the fight against extinction , science writer Justine E. @@136819239 <h> New research challenges the narrative of this country as classless , highlighting the importance of enabling children to realise their full potential . By Andrew Leigh . <h> Social mobility is key to Australian growth <p> In My Brilliant Career , Miles Franklin gave Australia a portrait of frustrated talent in the figure of Sybylla Melvyn . Sybylla is intelligent , ambitious , restless and painfully aware of the narrow world around her . She knows she has ability and she can see how few doors are open to a girl in her position . Her family 's fortunes are sliding , money is scarce , and marriage to a wealthier man is held out as the respectable route upwards . She refuses it . The book 's title is ironic : this is not the story of a brilliant career fulfilled but of one blocked at the outset . <p> More than a century on , we still argue about the same question in different language . How tightly should a person 's future be tethered to their parents ' income , their suburb , their school , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ should a childhood predict ? <p> As a politician , I see that as a question of fairness . As an economist , I see it as a question of efficiency . A country is less productive when it does a poor job of finding talent , nurturing talent and deploying talent . Social mobility is not only about justice between citizens . It is also about whether we are making full use of the abilities of our own people . <p> That matters because talent is common . Opportunity is not . <p> Australians like to tell ourselves a flattering story . We are not aristocratic , we say . We are not a society of fixed ranks . We are a place where a child from modest beginnings can make something of themselves . There is enough truth in that story to keep it alive -- but we could do better . <p> Australia performs respectably by international standards on intergenerational mobility . The latest research suggests that , compared with many advanced countries , the link between parents ' earnings and children 's later earnings is weaker @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mean that we can relax . In a recent Australian study , Tomas Kennedy and Peter Siminski found that absolute mobility , the simple question of whether children out-earn their parents , has slipped over time . More than 80 per cent of Baby Boomers earnt more than their parents at a comparable age . For Australians born in the late 1970s and early 1980s , that figure is closer to two-thirds . <p> Some of that reflects slower growth . Some reflects wider inequality . Both make it harder for a country to keep faith in the promise that each generation will have a broader horizon than the one before . <p> A country that makes better use of the abilities of its people will usually be fairer . It will also usually be richer . <p> Economists once told themselves the story that we did n't need to worry much about inequality , because society was so mobile . It did not matter much if some started high and others low , so long as children could move easily up and down the ladder . As economists have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ harsher story . Countries with greater inequality tend also to have less mobility . As the rungs on the ladder stretch further apart , it becomes harder to climb up or down . Summing up his team 's findings , US economist Raj Chetty notes : " Your chances of achieving the American dream are almost two times higher ... if you are growing up in Canada than in the United States . " <p> Australia is more mobile and more egalitarian than the US , but we still have plenty of room to improve . Boosting mobility is n't just good for fairness -- it can also lift the productivity of the economy . <p> Economists are used to thinking about misallocation across companies and industries . We worry when capital is trapped in weak businesses , or when workers are stuck in jobs that make poor use of their skills . Social mobility asks us to think about misallocation across lives . How much ability lies dormant because a child grew up in unstable housing , poor health , or a neighbourhood cut off from jobs and useful @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , engagement , skill and judgement , it 's vital that we encourage talent to flourish . Just as professional sporting teams benefit from youth feeder leagues and talent scouts , economies succeed when they seek out ability in unexpected places . A society that draws its inventors , entrepreneurs , managers and professionals from too narrow a slice of the population is leaving productive capacity idle . <p> The evidence on innovation is particularly strong . <p> US research shows that children from the richest 1 per cent of families are 10 times more likely to become inventors than children from below-median households , even when you compare children with similar maths performance early in life . The problem is not a shortage of inventive ability . The problem is that some children are much more likely to encounter the classrooms , mentors , institutions and expectations that turn ability into achievement . <p> Australia has its own version of that story . The latest Startup Muster survey on new climate technology suggests that only about one in nine founders come from lower socioeconomic backgrounds . We might think @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Elizabeth Blackburns : children with the native ability to transform burns medicine or molecular biology , whose paths never cross the teachers or mentors that would have let that ability flower . That 's not just a gross inequity , it 's a productivity loss . <p> Mobility can no longer be confined to academic debates among philosophers , sociologists and economists . The newer research -- looking at health , place , peers and connection -- has direct policy implications . <p> Consider neighbourhoods . Australian work using de-identified tax data has examined more than 300,000 cases of families moving during childhood . Researcher Nathan Deutscher finds that where a child grows up has a lasting effect on adult outcomes , including income and education . Timing matters too . Moving earlier tends to have larger effects than moving later . Opportunity , in other words , is rooted in streets , schools , sporting clubs , public transport links and local expectations . <p> This should shift the way we think about housing . <p> Housing is not only critical for wellbeing and wealth . In many cases @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ high-opportunity neighbourhoods . It decides which children are near stronger schools , safer streets , better services and richer social networks . The cost of a home is becoming the fee charged for entry to a better life . <p> In the first two decades of the 21st century , Australia failed to build enough homes . The result was higher rents , higher prices and a tighter grip of inherited advantage -- stored in land and passed on . Building more homes eases pressure on buyers and renters , makes it easier for workers to live near where the jobs are and creates more opportunities for children . <p> The same goes for early childhood and health . If a child arrives at school with chronic illness or untreated trauma , they are already carrying a heavier load than their classmates . That has consequences for fairness and for the shape of the labour force two decades later . The making of a productive economy starts well before the first pay packet -- it begins in homes , clinics , preschools and playgrounds . <p> This is not to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia has no shortage of such stories . But public policy should not be built on heroic exceptions . The task is not to admire those who scramble over the wall . It is to ask why the wall is there in the first place and how to bring it down . <p> There is an old tendency in public debate to separate growth from fairness , as though one belongs to hard-headed economists and the other to soft-hearted idealists . Social mobility exposes the falsity of that divide . A country that makes better use of the abilities of its people will usually be fairer . It will also usually be richer . <p> Mobility is important for economic policy , because wasted ability is an economic failure . The title My Brilliant Career still carries a warning . Australia has no shortage of talent or ambition . The challenge is to open more doors , in more suburbs , for more children . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on May 2 , 2026 as " Opportunity knocks " . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . The famous Gulf Stream is a surface current that is part of AMOC and also driven by trade winds . <p> Advertisement <p> This is the climate driver that keeps the weather in Europe and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : New York City is at roughly the same latitude as Portugal , and Nova Scotia in Canada is equivalent to northern Spain and southern France . <p> The Antarctic version of the AMOC -- sometimes called the Southern Meridional Overturning Circulation ( SMOC ) , Antarctic Meridional Overturning Circulation ( AntMOC ) or Antarctic Abyssal Overturning Circulation ( AAOC ) -- is less well known , but just as important . <p> The Antarctic overturning system plays a significant role in the circulation of nutrients back to the surface . This allows phytoplankton -- a building block of the food chain -- to thrive and absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis . Phytoplankton consume an estimated 40 per cent of all greenhouse emissions , about four times as much as the Amazon rainforest . <p> A growing number of scientists believe the AMOC could be reaching a tipping point where the system will sharply weaken or collapse this century . Matthew England , scientia professor at the University of NSW and deputy director of the Australian Centre for Excellence in Antarctic Science ( ACEAS ) , says in the past @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " You would n't get a Day After Tomorrow disaster movie ice age scenario under future climate change because the world will be so much hotter , " England said . " But an AMOC collapse would create a major climate disruption , with severe consequences for agriculture and social systems . " <p> A shutdown of AMOC would mean a more La Nina-like world , England says , with more flooding rains over eastern Australia and worse droughts and bushfire seasons over the south-west United States . <p> Turning off AMOC would not only make Europe much colder than it is at present , but it would also lead to substantial oceanic carbon release , says a March 2026 article in Communications Earth &amp; Environment . As a global average , this would lead to about 0.2 degrees of additional warming , but regional effects would vary -- the Arctic would be 7 degrees cooler and Antarctica would be 6 degrees warmer . <p> Predictions for AMOC range from a modest decline to full collapse by 2100 . The projections used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to 39 per cent , depending on the emissions scenario . <p> An April 2026 study in Science Advances suggests the AMOC is most likely to slow by about 50 per cent by 2100 . <p> A March 2026 paper in Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews : Climate Change finds that the AMOC has already weakened by about 15 per cent since the mid-20th century , and could be at a tipping point that could see it transition to a substantially weaker or collapsed state . <p> An eventual AMOC collapse might be already unavoidable , even under moderate climate change , the paper says . England , a co-author of the Wiley paper , says this is a system that has been stable for thousands of years . <h> How does it work ? <p> Sea ice in the polar regions forms in winter and melts in summer . Multi-year ice survives the summer months , but the overall area grows and contracts . <p> When the sea ice forms , only the water freezes . The salt is forced out , and the resulting brine falls to the depths of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bottom of the ocean is extremely dense because it is so cold and salty . <p> Pushing denser water to the bottom of the ocean displaces the water that is already there , causing upwelling . The strong westerly winds in the Southern Ocean also contribute to upwelling . <p> Upwelling and downwelling are linked in a continuous loop known as an overturning circulation . This exchanges colder abyssal water with warmer surface water , and brings nutrients from the ocean depths back to the surface . <p> Downwelling ( or sinking ) portions of the overturning circulations occur in both polar regions , one near Greenland and the other near Antarctica . They are linked through ocean currents as one giant global conveyor belt , but they also have localised effects . <p> " Around Antarctica , we 're talking about less than 1 per cent of the total area of the global ocean , yet these isolated polar waters control the circulation and properties of half the world 's ocean by volume , " England said . <p> The AMOC takes cold water that sinks in both the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Americas via deep ocean currents . Completing the loop , currents carry warm tropical surface water from the Gulf of Mexico past the East Coast of the United States to the North Atlantic . <p> Antarctic bottom water is the densest and fills the bottom two to three kilometres of the world 's oceans . Atlantic deep water is not as dense , and it fills the water column at depths of 1500 to 4000 metres . <h> How the overturning circulations replenish nutrients in the oceans <p> Nutrients near the surface of the ocean support life . Inorganic nutrients are consumed by phytoplankton , which absorb carbon dioxide and provide the building blocks of the food chain . <p> Dissolved organic matter is broken down by microbes , regenerating nutrients . Particles of organic matter such as dead organisms and faecal matter fall to the ocean floor because of gravity , making the deepest waters nutrient rich . <p> When the upwelling occurs , it spreads the nutrients from the bottom water back through the water column . <p> Turning off the Antarctic overturning circulation would give warmer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lead to more ice melt . In what is known as a " feedback loop " , the extra meltwater would further slow down the overturning . <p> The oceans and near surface air are already heating up -- up to 3 degrees in the Arctic and between 0.5 and 2 degrees across most of the globe . @@136847370 <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access . <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All other in your area <p> While it remains to be seen what the budget will hold , a fiscally constrained year ahead seems likely for the APS . The public sector union , the CPSU , has been vocal in expressing concern about job cuts across the service . <p> So what do federal public servants need to know about their workplace rights , lest they find themselves on the agency chopping block ? <p> The starting point , as always , is the Public Service Act 1999 , the legislation which governs public sector employment . <p> Section 29 of that law provides significant discretion for dismissing employees ; it says that an agency head " may at any time , by notice in writing , terminate the employment of an APS employee in the Agency . " <p> The provision then sets out the grounds for termination , which , in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Conduct and under performance , include " the employee is excess to the requirements of the Agency " . <p> The next place to look is the enterprise agreement of the relevant agency . We will use the Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water ( DCCEEW ) as an example . Due to common term bargaining across the APS , most enterprise agreements across the public service are very similar . <p> So far , most redundancies have been voluntary - we are yet to see widespread involuntary redundancies . Voluntary redundancy requirements at DCCEEW are set out in the enterprise agreement . <p> A delegate can invite an employee declared excess to requirements to consider voluntary redundancy ; the employee will then have a month to consider . The department is required to advise the employee of the amount of severance pay , payment in lieu of notice and leave entitlements and implications for their superannuation . Employees considering a voluntary redundancy are eligible for up to $600 to obtain financial advice . <p> If an employee accepts the voluntary redundancy , they are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some cases - or payment in lieu . They are also entitled to a voluntary redundancy benefit of two weeks ' salary for each year of service , with a minimum sum of four weeks , and a maximum of 48 weeks . <p> Redundancy payments are generously taxed , too , helping ease the blow for public servants made redundant . There is a tax-free threshold , which varies depending on length of service . <p> An employee declared excess , who elects not to take a voluntary redundancy , is then moved into a retention period - of 30 weeks ' duration for most staff , or a year , for staff over 45 or with more than 20 years ' service . <p> During this time , the department is required to assist the employee find alternative employment - this includes being placed on a priority internal placement register , and providing access to career transition support . <p> During the retention period , a public servant is required to take reasonable steps to seek a new role . They must " actively participate in learning and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assist in obtaining a permanent placement " , according to DCCEEW 's enterprise agreement . <p> After the retention period , if the employee has not found alternative employment , they will have their employment involuntarily terminated - with equivalent notice requirements to voluntary redundancies . <p> Provided APS employees have been engaged for more than six months , they are protected from unfair dismissal and can bring a claim with the Fair Work Commission in the event they consider they have been unfairly dismissed . A genuine redundancy will not be unfair dismissal . <p> To determine if a redundancy is genuine , the Commission will ask whether , in addition to complying with the enterprise agreement consultation obligations , " the person 's employer no longer required the person 's job to be performed by anyone because of changes in the operational requirements of the employer 's enterprise . " A redundancy will not be genuine if it would have been " reasonable in all the circumstances for the person to be redeployed " . <p> The High Court recently expanded the breadth of the inquiry into what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to redeploy staff . <p> Obviously , an APS agency does not have carte blanche to make staff redundant , even if they comply with these obligations . If that redundancy is motivated by unlawful discrimination , or because the public servant raised concerns about their employment conditions , or because they blew the whistle under the Public Interest Disclosure Act , it might be unlawful and give rise to claims under relevant laws . <p> However , subject to those limitations , and the procedural and consultation obligations under employment law and found in APS enterprise agreements , government departments have broad discretion to pursue redundancy programs . <p> That means that the latest federal budget will be one to watch for public servants . <p> Whatever the outlook , though , APS workers can take some solace in the relatively generous entitlements available in the event of redundancy . <p> John Wilson is the managing legal director at BAL Lawyers and an accredited specialist in industrial relations and employment law . <p> Kieran Pender is an honorary senior lecturer at the ANU Law School and a consultant at BAL Lawyers .

@@136871812 <p> The findings , published Monday in Nature Climate Change , show that colored micro- and nanoplastics suspended in the atmosphere may contribute to global warming at a level equal to 16% of that caused by black carbon , or soot . The study adds to mounting evidence that plastic pollution does n't just degrade terrestrial and marine ecosystems -- it can also influence Earth 's climate . <p> Prior to this research , " we really did n't know if these things were even warming or cooling , " co-author Drew Shindell , Nicholas Distinguished Professor of Earth Science at Duke University , said during a press briefing . He worked with a team of atmospheric chemists at Fudan University , led by Professor Hongbo Fu , to precisely measure how microplastics interact with light . Their analysis revealed that the net atmospheric effect of almost all microplastics across a range of optical properties is warming . <h> Microplastics everywhere , even in the air <p> Plastic pollution on land and in the ocean gradually breaks down into micro- and nanoplastics , and these particles are so light that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Atmospheric plastic concentrations are particularly high over ocean gyres , large systems of rotating ocean currents where plastic accumulates and degrades as pieces bump into each other . For example , the North Pacific Garbage Patch -- an enormous floating island of trash between Hawaii and California -- is created by the North Pacific Gyre . <p> Much remains unknown about the concentration and distribution of microplastics throughout the global atmosphere , but in recent years , researchers have been investigating their direct radiative forcing : how they change the balance of energy ( or heat ) flowing in and out of the atmosphere . This is an important metric for measuring how a gas or an aerosol drives climate change , as those with a heat-trapping effect help global temperatures rise . <h> How microplastics are heating the atmosphere <p> A 2021 study published in Nature used previous estimates of how colored microplastics absorb and scatter sunlight to calculate their radiative forcing . The results suggested that these particles have a negligible effect on Earth 's climate -- especially when compared with the overall impact of other aerosols @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their influence will intensify as plastic pollution worsens . <p> This new study used a more systematic approach to refine the direct radiative forcing of colored microplastics . Fu and his colleagues used high-resolution electron spectroscopy and atmospheric transport simulations to analyze their optical properties , finding their warming potential to be much higher than the 2021 estimate . <p> On a global scale , this warming effect is still relatively small . But over ocean regions with high concentrations of plastic , such as the North Pacific Garbage Patch , it can exceed that of black carbon by nearly a factor of 5 . <p> Zamin Kanji , an atmospheric scientist and lecturer at ETH Zurich who was not involved in the study , said the findings are not altogether surprising . " If the plastic particles start to be present in significant amounts , they are bound to have effects on direct and indirect radiative forcing , " he told Gizmodo in an email . <p> However , " the fact that the concentrations of micro- and nanoplastics that we detect in airborne samples is increasing -- as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- is definitely worrying , " he said . <p> Kanji noted that key uncertainties remain about where airborne microplastics are found globally , how different particle sizes are distributed in the atmosphere , and how their physical and chemical properties change over time . The study 's authors acknowledge these limitations but emphasize that their findings clearly point to atmospheric microplastics as a warming agent . <p> " We 're really confident now that we understand their optics and their net effect on radiation , but we 're not as confident -- and we need more measurements from all around the world -- to really characterize more precisely how much of the stuff is in the atmosphere , " Shindell said .

@@136903522 <p> The findings , published Monday in Communications Sustainability , show that renewable energy is far more cost-effective than direct air capture -- a growing carbon removal strategy -- at reducing atmospheric carbon . Across nearly every U.S. region through 2050 , money spent deploying wind or solar power will deliver a greater combined climate and public health benefit than if it is spent on direct air capture , according to the study . <p> " Our study basically asks , if someone has $100 million they are willing to invest in reducing CO2 in the atmosphere , what is the best way for them to spend this money ? " senior author Jonathan J. Buonocore , an assistant professor of environmental health at Boston University , told Gizmodo in an email . <p> " We found that $100 million will reduce much more CO2 if this was invested in wind or solar , especially in coal-heavy grids in the U.S. , than if it was invested in direct air capture , " he explained . " Also , investing in renewables will reduce air pollution , which direct air @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Carbon removal and renewable energy generation approach the climate crisis from two opposing angles . Transitioning from fossil fuels to clean power sources prevents more carbon from entering the atmosphere , while carbon removal reduces the amount of carbon that 's already in the atmosphere . The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has determined that both strategies will be essential to stabilizing CO2-induced global surface temperature rise . <p> There are several ways to pull carbon out of the atmosphere . Earth 's ecosystems do this naturally , storing captured atmospheric carbon in soils , forests , and the ocean . Humans can enhance these natural carbon sinks through various interventions , but as the climate crisis has rapidly intensified , technologies like direct air capture have emerged as a more aggressive way to reduce atmospheric carbon . <p> The trouble is , direct air capture remains underdeveloped due to its prohibitively high cost , energy demand , and the need to scale manufacturing . Still , this technology is increasingly recognized as a necessary near-term complement to phasing out emissions . And since climate mitigation resources are limited @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> DAC ca n't compete yet <p> To figure out whether direct air capture could be cost competitive with renewable energy ( specifically wind and solar ) , Buonocore and his colleagues modeled the climate and public health benefits of each strategy for the same amount of dollars spent . <p> The researchers monetized climate benefits using the social cost of carbon : the dollar amount equivalent to the long-term damage done by one ton of CO2 emissions in a given year . For public health , they used a model to estimate avoided air pollution exposure and reduced mortality risk , then monetized those benefits using the value of a statistical life -- the same metric used by the Environmental Protection Agency . <p> Because direct air capture is still in its infancy , the researchers modeled its benefits under four different efficiency improvement scenarios ranging from its current commercial performance ( which requires 5,500 kilowatt-hours of electricity and $1,000 to capture one ton of CO2 ) to a " breakthrough " scenario ( 800 kWh and $100 per ton of captured CO2 ) , which is at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Only under the ' breakthrough ' scenario , which would involve efficiency improving by a factor of approximately 7 , and cost dropping to 10% of what it is currently , does direct air capture perform better than renewables , " Buonocore said . <p> Part of the problem is that direct air capture only removes CO2 from the atmosphere . By replacing fossil fuels , renewable energy reduces emissions of fine particulate matter , nitrogen oxides , sulfur dioxide , and other hazardous air pollutants . Thus , direct air capture offers a smaller public health benefit . In fact , under the current commercial performance scenario , grid-connected direct air capture produced more greenhouse gases and air pollution damage through 2050 than it offset . <p> To be clear , Buonocore and his colleagues are not arguing that we should abandon direct air capture , but their study emphasizes the importance of prioritizing renewable energy investments in the near-term . <p> " Our work here indicates that it would be more cost-effective to deploy renewables and likely do other decarbonization to basically ' stop the flow ' of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be necessary to clean up the excess CO2 after most other major sources of CO2 have been stopped . " 
@@136903523 <p> The fossil fuel industry is responsible for more than a third of the world 's methane pollution , and its emissions show no sign of falling . According to a new report , fixing methane leaks at oil and gas sites is not only essential to curbing global warming , but could also bolster energy security amid the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran . <p> The International Energy Agency 's Global Methane Tracker 2026 report , published Monday , estimates that oil , gas , and coal production -- which reached record levels in 2025 -- emits 124 million metric tons of methane per year . Harnessing those emissions could make more than 7 trillion cubic feet ( 200 billion cubic meters ) of natural gas available to the global energy sector annually . <p> The IEA acknowledges that it would take time to build the necessary equipment and infrastructure to achieve such massive additions , but the potential is there . In the nearer term , nearly 530 billion cubic feet ( 15 billion cubic meters ) of natural gas could become available to markets " very @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ existing export capacity implement readily-accessible methane abatement measures across their gas systems , the report states . <h> Wasting a valuable resource <p> Methane is one of the most potent greenhouse gases , with a global warming potential roughly 30 times greater than that of CO2 over a 100-year period . It also happens to be the primary component of natural gas , a highly valuable and heavily traded global fuel commodity . <p> The extraction and processing of fossil fuels spews massive amounts of methane into the atmosphere , driving up global temperatures and wasting a resource that could be made into natural gas . Capturing these emissions would go a long way toward mitigating climate change and strengthening global energy security , and there is an urgent need to do both . <p> The war in Iran has triggered a global fossil fuel energy crisis . According to the IEA , the effective closure of the Straight of Hormuz has removed roughly 20% of global liquefied natural gas supply from the market . The long-term natural gas additions outlined in the report would be double the supply volumes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " This is not only a climate issue : there are also major energy security benefits that can come from tackling methane and flaring , especially at a time when the world is urgently looking for additional supply amid the current crisis , " IEA Chief Energy Economist Tim Gould said in a statement . <h> How to harness methane emissions <p> Of course , if capturing the fossil fuel industry 's wasted methane was a no-brainer , we 'd be doing it already . According to the Environmental Protection Agency , there are several reasons why efforts to harness and profitably use this resource are not widespread across the industry . <p> For one , methane emissions are a byproduct of industrial process and have not historically been viewed as an energy resource in its own right . Emitters also might not be familiar with the technologies available for methane recovery or the potential for profitable recovery projects , particularly in developing countries . What 's more , many energy markets fail to incentivize investment in methane recovery . <p> Despite all this , the IEA report makes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from fossil fuel extraction and processing facilities . Based on average energy prices in 2025 , the IEA claims that roughly 30% of methane emissions from fossil fuels could be abated at no cost with existing technology , as the market value of the captured gas would exceed the required capital and operating costs of abatement . <p> " The economics look even more attractive in 2026 , as fuel prices come under upward pressure from the conflict in the Middle East , " the report states . <p> Whether the current fuel crisis will finally motivate the fossil fuel industry to make good use of its methane emissions remains to be seen . What is clear is that the tools to do so already exist , and the stakes -- for both climate and energy security -- have never been higher .
