@@137036616 <h> Kacey Musgraves , one of the most interesting voices in contemporary country music , goes back to basics on her new album , Middle of Nowhere . By Shaad D'Souza . <h> Kacey Musgraves returns with Middle of Nowhere <p> Few careers in country music over the past decade-plus have been as interesting as Kacey Musgraves ' . The Texas-born singer broke through in 2013 with her album Same Trailer Different Park , a record that was traditionalist in sound but , in comparison with the conservative Nashville firmament , almost confrontationally left-wing . That album 's calling-card single , " Follow Your Arrow " , was banned by country radio and censored at the Country Music Association Awards for its casual support of gay rights . " So make lots of noise ( hey ) / Kiss lots of boys ( yup ) / Or kiss lots of girls , if that 's something you 're into , " she sang on the track -- hardly shocking but enough to establish Musgraves as a rabble-rouser in the politically buttoned-up world of country . <p> Since then Musgraves has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ second album , Pageant Material , seemingly alluded to her rebellious spirit -- its primary themes were her proclivity for smoking weed and her loner tendencies -- and found huge acclaim from indie music outlets such as Spin and Pitchfork . Golden Hour , which followed in 2018 , marked the beginning of her experimentation with genres such as pop and disco and , although it was still recognisable as a country album , found Musgraves a new mainstream audience who appreciated her wit and the spaciousness of her arrangements . <p> In an unlikely upset , Golden Hour became the first country album in nearly a decade to win Album of the Year at the Grammys . Its enormous popularity suggested a future in which Musgraves might have gone down the path of many country crossover stars before her , towards pop music . <p> She kind of did that -- her follow-up , 2021 's Star-Crossed , expanded her purview beyond country into yacht rock , programmed beats and the kind of arch kiss-offs that have become common in pop in recent years . Star-Crossed was seen as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ do n't think it 's because of the slight pivot towards pop . I think the bitterness of her lyrics on that record , written about her divorce from the man who inspired the lovestruck , magnanimous Golden Hour , alienated listeners who preferred Musgraves for her space-cadet optimism . On the tour in support of Star-Crossed , Musgraves took to inserting ad-libs into the Golden Hour songs that suggested she no longer felt aligned with their declarations of everlasting love , making for a bizarre vibe . <p> Perhaps Musgraves herself felt these tides swaying against her new direction , because since Star-Crossed she has seemed suspiciously like a star in retrenchment mode . First came 2024 's Deeper Well , a coolly received folk record that lacked the needling hooks of Musgraves ' prior albums and suggested that , a few years post break-up , she had embraced alternative spirituality as a way of finding life 's meaning . The problem was that it 's not particularly compelling to hear a star with such a witty eye for detail write about crystals and astrology . She may have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fame " , but the record 's whole vibe was that of someone interested in salvaging their reputation as a sensitive , more rustic star . <p> Middle of Nowhere may be an obvious choice , but there is no denying that Musgraves remains one of country 's sharpest , most engaging writers . <p> Two years on , Musgraves has released Middle of Nowhere . Thanks to sturdier arrangements and more dynamic hooks , her new album achieves the goals of its predecessor fairly successfully . Understated , funny and groovy in a way that recalls Musgraves ' best albums , Middle of Nowhere may be an obvious choice , but there is no denying upon listening that she remains one of country 's sharpest , most engaging writers . It affirms that the slightly unlikeable Deeper Well may have just been a blip . Musgraves sounds energised and tapped-in here , and although not all her witticisms land -- " Dry Spell " , a single about sexual frustration that 's too laboured by half , feels like Musgraves attempting to write an " old Kacey Musgraves " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to her vision of small-town America . <p> The " middle of nowhere " of the album 's title is a fantastical composite place . Musgraves said she spent time in Tennessee and Mexico , as well as her home town of Golden , Texas , between releases , and she fills this album with figures seemingly taken straight from country iconography . She subverts tropes of the male drifter on " Abilene " , singing about a woman who " went out for cigarettes , ended up on a bus / Headed somewhere , did n't really care " . On " Mexico Honey " , she 's a girl in hot-pink shorts , with not a care in the world , dancing for a guy she met in a bar . The mythic-seeming animal of " Coyote " represents the dying embers of a relationship , while " Back on the Wagon " finds bitter humour in the story of a woman dating an alcoholic . <p> Musgraves ' career has focused more and more on herself since Golden Hour . While many of the songs that trawl @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ two records was her savvy ability to write characters that seemed both outlandish and believable . That skill is still razor-sharp on many of the songs on Middle of Nowhere , and sometimes Musgraves seemingly applies it to herself , too . This album , she 's said , was inspired by solitude and a lengthy period of singledom , and she manages to both specify and universalise those feelings . On " Loneliest Girl " , a buoyant pop-country song that feels like a more mature update of the songs on Pageant Material , she sings about enjoying life alone : " Y'all do n't need to worry about what I might be missing / Put me on a poster of somebody who 's living the life / Yeah , I 'm alright / I ai n't even mad at all the people in love . " <p> Musically , Musgraves says this album explores the outer boundaries of country as a genre . Although it does n't feel particularly far outside her comfort zone -- it 's neither radical nor jaw-dropping -- it is exciting to hear her @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ like " Horses and Divorces " , a collaboration with the famed country singer Miranda Lambert who is in many ways one of Musgraves ' clearest forebears . <p> The track , a classic call-and-response duet , sprinkles a little tabloid fuel on the otherwise unbothered Middle of Nowhere . The lyrics of " Horses and Divorces " allude to a minor feud that dates back to Musgraves ' first album : " There were chips on our shoulders , but now that we 're older / It 's all whiskey under the bridge , " they sing in unison . It 's a classic conceit for a country song given a canny update for an era of pop that thrives on conflict and unspoken drama , but it never feels like Musgraves is simply reaching out to Lambert in search of a headline that will juice sales . <p> Middle of Nowhere reveals how good Musgraves is at projecting authenticity and calm in a genre that claims to prize these things but often comes across as contrived . That 's especially true for " Uncertain , TX " , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the record 's strongest tracks . A kiss-off to an unruly ex , the song sounds both urgent and unbothered : " It 's weird that such a tiny town / Would have such a large amount / Of cowboys that just ca n't get off the fence , " she sings , never letting bitterness infect the song 's easy sway . At the end , she lets rip a typically Musgraves ad-lib : " Down here in Uncertain , Texas / Nobody ever makes up their dusty , old , love-bombin ' , snake-charmin ' , bullshittin ' , heartbreakin ' , godforsaken , dumb-ass mind . " It feels like a future karaoke classic , charmingly breezy in its approach and hilariously cutthroat in its sentiment . <p> Middle of Nowhere is n't likely to cause the splash of the albums that arrived in the immediate wake of Golden Hour . But that does n't seem to be the point : rather , it feels like Musgraves ' attempt to reassert the core of her artistic practice after a few years of searching and experimentation . @@137036618 <h> Yumna Kassab Goodbye , My Love <p> This is a story of a marital separation and divorce between Amina and Amin . Though there was a small period of grace , back when " the peace stretched between them more than the arguments " , it seemed that from the outset , their relationship was marred by constant conflict . Disagreement infects their everyday lives , from the kind of furniture they prefer to the possible names and number of their future children . They seem to take great delight in cutting each other down , deriding each other 's choices in wardrobe , personal habits and life philosophies . Maintaining public " shopfront " behaviour proves too arduous , considering " the slippery surfaces , the trip hazards in the back " . Tension even follows them when they are on holidays and staying at an expensive seaside resort . <p> Each chapter in Goodbye , My Love consists of only a page or two and is written in the third person and from the point of view of Amina , who is determined to finally leave an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Yumna Kassab 's prose is flat , unadorned and unmoored with markers of place or time . There are no descriptive flourishes . The reader does not know what the warring protagonists look like . <p> Kassab may be trying for a generalist , universal effect , an everyman 's and everywoman 's experience of rupture and pain in a marriage and its eventual dissolution , but the lack of detail makes the novel unsatisfying . It 's hard to feel much for either character when they seem to be generic archetypes rather than individual portraits . In such a short , spare book , there 's also a surprising amount of repetition that does nothing to further the narrative . <p> Despite her affluent background -- she has access to servants and a driver -- Amina constantly bemoans her circumstances and her solipsistic outlook becomes a self-indulgent exercise in airing her grievances . @@137036620 <h> The appointment of a minister for men and boys in Victoria is a first in Australia , demonstrating a political willingness to engage with the harms of online misogyny . By Hannah Bambra . <h> Victoria 's new minister for men and boys to focus on schools <p> When Paul Edbrooke was working as a special education teacher in Frankston in the early 2000s , mobile phones were simple Nokias used for texting or a quick game of Snake . Tamagotchis and Pok ? mon cards were being banned from schools , as they were considered too distracting and competitive . <p> Twenty-six years later , young people are reported to spend an average of 4.8 hours on social media and have up to nine hours of screen time each day . Australian children as young as 10 are showing signs of addictive screen-related disorders . <p> This is the world in which Edbrooke has become the country 's first minister for men and boys . The Victorian portfolio has a dual remit , addressing men 's mental health and wellbeing alongside combating the amplification of online misogyny . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ right-wing influencers such as Andrew Tate and the wider incel movement , a women-hating online subculture that takes its name from a shortened form of the phrase " involuntarily celibate " . <p> Research from earlier this year showed that Gen Z men were twice as likely as Baby Boomers to think women should " obey their husbands " . Almost a quarter thought women should not appear " too self-sufficient " . <p> " When boys do n't have a positive story about what it means to be a man , they go looking for one -- and what they find , especially online , is often harmful to them and their loved ones , " Edbrooke tells The Saturday Paper . <p> " That 's why we 're talking to men , families and organisations on the frontline to identify new approaches to men 's health and wellbeing that give Victorian men and boys a positive story about who they are and what they can be . " <p> Victorian premier Jacinta Allan announced the role six weeks after the airing of Louis Theroux 's documentary Inside the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ societal shift " in how boys are supported . <p> Daniel Principe , a youth advocate and educator who has spoken to more than 50,000 boys across Australia , says manosphere-style messages have entered the mainstream . <p> " Almost all boys from Year 6 upwards are seeing content that says they should be dominant and women should be submissive , " Principe says . <p> Research shows that men who strongly adhere to rigid , dominance-based ideals of masculinity are more than eight times as likely to use violence against an intimate partner in the long term . <p> " It is telling them they are not manly enough , not muscly enough , not a ' high-value male ' . It creates no space where you could be authentic , where you are known as a guy who is respectful , decent and trustworthy -- it casts that all aside and labels it as weakness . " <p> When Principe asks primary school-aged boys what they love most about their father figures , their number one reply is " that he spends time with me " . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pushing the opposite message on men and teens -- that all you need to do is earn money , instead of focusing on being a kind and caring person , " he says . <p> National mental health charity Beyond Blue says that rigid ideas about masculinity , defining it as being strong or self-reliant , can also shape how some men respond when they 're struggling . <p> About one in three young men experiences a mental disorder in any given year , with depression affecting about one in 10 Australians aged 15-24 . ? Nine people per day die by suicide in Australia and 75 per cent of those are men . Considerably fewer men seek support for mental health problems , as reported by the Australian Bureau of Statistics ' most recent national study on mental health and wellbeing . <p> In New South Wales , Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane has created a shadow men 's health portfolio , citing disproportionate suicide rates , depression and other comorbidities . @@137088201 <h> What happens in budget lockup <p> About 1.30pm today , hundreds of journalists will reluctantly hand over their phones , disconnect from the internet and spend the next six hours locked up in specially prepared newsrooms in Canberra , Sydney and beyond . <p> It 's budget day , the busiest of the year for political journalists , and reporters have to sign up to a range of legal requirements ( and submit to a few arcane rituals ) just to get their foot in the door . <p> Treasurer Jim Chalmers arrives at Parliament House for an interview ahead of the budget.Alex Ellinghausen <h> Preparing the document <p> The federal budget is a gigantic undertaking , with the first planning meetings of cabinet 's Expenditure Review Committee taking place in September . Hundreds of officials are involved in planning , developing , writing and running it . <p> Advertisement <p> Major themes for the budget start to be nailed down during the quiet weeks in January , and by March-April major decisions are being finalised in portfolios . <p> In the weeks before the budget , the attending @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some tick and flick : everyone signs a legally binding contract pledging not to breach the embargo . <p> Loading <p> Budget day for journalists is the moment , after months of work by government behind the scenes ( and weeks of both deliberate leaks and unauthorised scoops ) , that the document is released into the wild for public judgement . <p> My first time locked up was in 2008 and early on I was incredibly nervous , terrified I would miss a crucial measure that a competitor would find . <p> Advertisement <p> The nerves eased around 2010 when I found myself in the line to enter lock up next to John Kehoe ( now the Australian Financial Review 's economics editor , but a baby journo at the time like me ) . <p> Kehoe looked at me and grinned as I explained my nerves and responded , in his laconic style , " it is a test , but we get to grade the government " . That helped . <h> Enter the storm <p> These days , I think of the budget day lockup as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a storm . <p> After weeks of frenzied activity in the lead up , journalists have all their electronic devices confiscated , lose internet access and all we can do is read the budget papers for six hours . <p> Advertisement <p> It 's a shrinkingly rare thing to have so much time to digest information , across the four main budget papers , the treasurer 's speech and the so-called " glossies " -- smaller booklets that outline major initiatives . It 's necessary to get through hundreds of pages . <h> Related Article <p> We are n't flying blind . Treasury officials set up their own desks in the gallery so they can answer questions about that anomaly we spotted in budget paper No.4 . <p> At 7.30pm , when the treasurer of the day rises to their feet in parliament to deliver their budget speech , the embargo lifts and we return to the world of electronic communications and constant updates . <p> Editors go into overdrive at this point , publishing and placing stories on the homepage , making final checks on print pages and keeping @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the Business Council to Greenpeace and the Academy of Science ( and hundreds of others ) deliver their verdicts . <p> Advertisement <p> The storm will continue for the next few weeks , at least , and the news out of Canberra will be dominated by budget stories that range from backlash , stories of government horse-trading to secure enough votes in the Senate for this-or-that piece of legislation , and more . <p> The aftermath of Joe Hockey 's horror 2014 budget lasted much longer , given how badly it was delivered and received . Arguably , the backlash did n't really finish until September 2015 , when Hockey and then-prime minister Tony Abbott were removed by the Liberal Party room . It was n't all Hockey 's fault , that one -- it was a real team effort . <h> What lock up used to be like ... and how it has changed <p> It 's crazy-busy , but also mundane . <p> Once upon a time , a couple of hundred journalists would gather in parliament 's massive main committee room and a few smaller committee @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canberra from head offices around the country armed with dozens of laptops ( and desktops before that ) that would be set up in private computer networks that could n't connect to the outside world -- but which could connect securely to computers in the head offices used to lay out pages and publish the next day 's newspaper . <p> The Canberra Times ' most junior reporter ( me at the time ) could end up seated one row over from ABC greats like Alan Kohler , Fran Kelly or Lyndal Curtis , or next to a reporter you 'd never met working for an outlet you 'd never heard of . <p> The buzz in the room was extraordinary , and hearing one of the big dogs from a rival organisation yell across the room their plans for their column or news trunk ( the main story of the day ) added a certain frisson . <p> Over cold pies , dodgy egg sandwiches and Allen 's snakes arrayed on a trolley out in a corridor , you 'd bump into The Age 's Michelle Grattan or The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what they thought of the budget , before agreeing profusely with whatever they said ( so you did n't sound stupid ) . <p> Advertisement <p> But COVID-19 put an end to the budget-day big room , and now people work from their own offices in the press gallery , which is level two on the Senate side of parliament . Lifts are shut down so you ca n't leave the press gallery , and treasury officials are assigned to bureaus to watch journalists closely to ensure that market-sensitive information is n't leaked from a hidden phone . <h> So what do you do in lock up ? <p> First , from 1.30pm , I read the start of budget paper No.1 , which contains key headline figures such as unemployment forecasts , inflation , the size of the surplus or deficit ( usually the latter ) and other key information . <h> Related Article <p> Then , I 'd read the treasurer 's speech to see what story they 're trying to tell Australians about the economic year ahead , and what their priorities are . Then , it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ details about the key measures announced by the government in terms of where they are spending and saving money in major departments . <p> Advertisement <p> Early on , I 'd read the glossies first , but while these sometimes contain some useful extra information such as case studies -- this tax cut will leave John Smith $1400 per year better off -- they tend to put a positive government spin on things . I now often leave them to last . <p> It 's a multimedia affair in lock-up . Months of technical work goes into working out how to do charts and graphics and illustrations and videos in a hermetically sealed environment . Our journalists step out from their interrogation of the numbers to record podcasts and film videos . Online interactives are built without access to online . Every camera and computer used is examined by treasury to make sure we can not communicate with the world outside until they say so . <p> By about 3pm , smokers and vapers are beginning to look at the emergency exit stair wells and bathroom smoke alarms , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and snakes have arrived . Sometimes , there 's sushi . <p> More importantly , senior editors and journalists are ready to have a phone hook up with head office to talk through what they believe the thrust of budget coverage should be -- and what should be top of the website that night and on the front page the next day . <p> Has the government kept its promises ? Has it abandoned any plans it had foreshadowed ? Are their any surprises in there that have n't been flagged ahead of time ? And , most importantly , is this budget in the national interest ? <p> Advertisement <p> Then it 's on to the treasurer and finance minister 's packed joint press conference , usually around 3.30pm and held in another committee room , in which journalists fire their first salvos and probe the two senior economic ministers about the document they 're about to release . <p> Almost inevitably , you have to sit through a PowerPoint slideshow before getting to the good bit , which is asking impertinent questions . <p> After that press conference @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stories . <p> But the politicians are not quite done with us . <h> The walk and talk <p> Advertisement <p> By about 4.30pm , the treasurer , finance minister and often the prime minister take a stroll through the press gallery to answer questions , put on the charm and try to glean what is going to end up on tomorrow 's front page . Anthony Albanese , Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher always take a stroll down the red-carpeted corridor on level two , and Treasury secretaries tend to do the same ( and make a beeline for Shane Wright ) . <p> I can still remember the smiles on the faces of Kevin Rudd and Wayne Swan as they walked through the main committee room in 2008 , proud of delivering the first Labor budget after more than a decade , even as economic storm clouds gathered . Likewise , the grins of Abbott and Hockey in 2014 as they confided to senior editors from a rival publication about a document they believed would have a major impact on the state of federal finances . <p> Impact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Former prime minister Tony Abbott and treasurer Joe Hockey prepare for the 2015 budget after their ill-fated first outing in 2014 . Andrew Meares <p> By 4.30pm onwards , people are filing their assigned stories and if they are n't , editors are hassling them because those stories need to be produced and those figures need to be checked well before the embargo lifts . <p> Advertisement <h> Related Article <p> Months of planning goes into this moment : almost everyone knows what they 'll be writing before they head into the budget , whether it be a piece of analysis , the trunk , a story in one of their rounds ( specialisations ) such as Defence , NDIS , climate change or something else . <p> A couple of journalists will enter the lockup knowing not much is likely to change in their round , so they 'll be writing one of our most popular stories -- the two-minute budget , winners and losers or what this budget means for you . <p> They 're also on standby in case a story we did n't expect is spotted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And we 're done <p> Advertisement <p> At around 7.30pm , the treasurer rises to their feet and the speech begins , and we can turn our phones back on to arrange catch-ups with colleagues and hear from the babysitter about what atrocities have been committed by our children while we 've been sealed off from the electric world . <p> Later that night , in bars in the Canberra suburbs of Kingston , Manuka and Barton , after-office dinners have concluded , journos will show their rivals a PDF of tomorrow 's front page and fret about a story they might have missed . <p> James Massola is chief political commentator . @@137088584 <p> When the Hunga Tonga -- Hunga Ha'apa submarine volcano erupted in 2022 , it spewed roughly 2.9 billion tons of ash and gas into the air above the South Pacific . According to a new study , the eruption also cleaned up some of its own mess . <p> The researchers estimate that the eruption released about 330 gigagrams of methane , which is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by more than 2 million cows . But their findings , published in Nature Communications on Thursday , show that chemical reactions within the eruption plume destroyed about 900 megagrams of methane per day -- roughly equivalent to the daily emissions from 2 million cows . As if that was n't surprising enough , they also found that the cloud kept removing its own methane pollution for 10 days as it drifted toward South America . <p> " It is known that volcanoes emit methane during eruptions , but until now it was not known that volcanic ash is also capable of partially cleaning up this pollution , " first author Maarten van Herpen of the Dutch organization @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ How volcanic eruptions emit and destroy methane <p> Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over a 20-year period . Scientists believe it currently drives about 30% of global warming . Fortunately , methane breaks down in the atmosphere relatively quickly , typically within 10 years . <p> Reducing methane emissions from industrial processes and agriculture will be essential to mitigating climate change , but not all methane emissions can be reduced . Some stem from natural processes such as microbial decomposition or , of course , volcanic eruptions . To address methane pollution from those sources and slow global warming in the near term , researchers are exploring ways to accelerate the natural breakdown of atmospheric methane . <p> This study uncovered a mechanism that could help them do just that . Using the TROPOMI imaging spectrometer aboard the European Space Agency 's Sentinel-5P satellite , the researchers determined that the eruption plume contained unusually high concentrations of formaldehyde , a short-lived intermediate that forms when methane breaks down . Formaldehyde only exists for a few hours before it decomposes into @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plume at high concentrations for more than a week , suggesting methane was continuously breaking down . <p> Previous research led by van Herpen showed that when dust from the Sahara Desert blows over the Atlantic Ocean , it mixes with sea spray to form iron salt aerosols . When sunlight interacts with these particles , it produces chlorine atoms that accelerate the decomposition of methane . He and his colleagues believe a similar reaction mechanism took place within the volcanic cloud ; seawater hurled into the atmosphere by the eruption mingled with ash , and the mixture reacted with sunlight to produce highly reactive chlorine atoms . <h> Turning this mechanism into a climate solution <p> The findings provide further evidence that this mechanism could help reduce atmospheric methane concentrations -- if engineers can figure out a safe , effective , and economically viable way to replicate it . <p> Researchers have already proposed some strategies , such as building reactors that pull methane from the air and bubble it through a chlorine-saturated brine or spraying chlorine atoms directly into the atmosphere via a controlled release system , though @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ key hurdle to developing these interventions is accurately measuring how much methane they remove . " How do you prove that methane has been removed from the atmosphere ? How do you know your method works ? It 's very difficult , " co-author Jos de Laat , a senior scientist at the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute , said in the statement . " But here we address that problem by showing that methane breakdown can in fact be observed using satellites . " <p> The researchers hope their findings will inspire more engineers to leverage chlorine atoms as a methane-removing agent and validate their approaches using satellite spectroscopy . As global warming rapidly accelerates , finding innovative ways to reduce atmospheric methane concentrations will only become more critical .

@@137121916 <h> " Like putting a cup into a holder : " Electric ships could soon be charging at sea <p> A consortium of Norwegian companies and research organisations have developed what they describe as a " plug and play " system for charging battery powered service vessels at sea . <p> The new magnetic inductive charging plug , described as easy to operate " as putting a cup in a cup holder " , has been spearheaded by Norwegian shipbuilder Vard and research institutes SINTEF and NORCE under the Ocean Charger project banner . <p> The Ocean Charger project aimed to develop and test a full-scale ship charging solution to enable emission-free service vessel operations , particularly for those servicing offshore wind farms , and the idea was to use the power generated by these wind farms to charge the vessels . <p> A heavy-duty traditional charging connection was tested through the early parts of Ocean Charger , but these chargers rely on exposed contact points that degrade after prolonged exposure to salty air . <p> " Movement and wear make charging at sea challenging when using a classic plug-based @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ VP research and innovation at Vard , who also headed up the large Ocean Charger project . " Mechanical wear and tear , corrosion and demanding maintenance increase the risk and costs . " <p> But researchers from Vard , alongside scientists and engineers in the Ocean Charger project , were able to develop a new charging connection which uses a magnetic inductive charger encapsulated in materials that can withstand offshore conditions . <p> " We 've looked at a lot of solutions here , " said Giuseppe Guidi , a senior research scientist at SINTEF . <p> " And we 've tested a possible solution that works almost like a regular electrical contact . But we can avoid all the problems because we transfer the power inductively by encapsulating the plug itself in materials that can withstand just about anything . " <p> The inductive charging solution consists of two parts -- a magnetic coil mounted on a cable stretches out from the charging station , which could be mounted on a wind turbine , and drops into a receptacle housing a second magnetic coil . <p> Electrical current @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ instead on a magnetic field generated when the two coils are properly aligned . <p> " It wo n't be necessary to be precise when lowering the plug into the receiver hole , " said Guidi . <p> " It 's almost like putting a cup in a cup holder . It will fit no matter which way it is turned . Very plug and play . " <p> The physical components are n't the only important parts of the process , however . Transferring power wirelessly from offshore charging infrastructure to a ship 's battery requires a range of technical solutions . <p> Power must be converted from alternating current to direct current , for example , sent at high voltage through a flexible cable , and then converted to high-frequency current that can be transmitted via the magnetic field . Onboard the vessel , that power must be captured , converted again , and transferred safely to the battery . <p> To accomplish all of this , and to withstand both high power and rough sea conditions , has been the focus of the Ocean Charger project . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at offshore wind farms , the Ocean Charge team also believe their new charging technology could also be used by platform supply vessels ( PSVs ) in use by the oil industry . <p> Joshua S. @@137154643 <h> The ' angertainment ' trap : Why you ca n't stop clicking on things that make you mad <p> " Angertainers " are exploiting the human instinct to seek threat -- and social media 's love of outrage -- to divide society rather than lift it , argues a communications expert . Is it time " rage bait " came with a warning label ? <p> " This is a BIG win in the culture war for America , " a social media influencer told her millions of followers last August , celebrating the decision of a restaurant chain to abandon plans to simplify its logo . <p> A logo change could destroy America ? Now that 's an idea you would n't have heard a few years ago . But in it , we can dissect all the ugly parts of a beast that has become the dominant political force of our time : we are living deep in an era of manufactured outrage . <p> A mainstay of highway rest stops in the American South , the restaurant chain Cracker Barrel has struggled in recent years with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ announced a refresh of its rustic , old-timey brand : dropping a decades-old drawing of a character known as Uncle Herschel sitting on a wooden chair and updating " Cracker Barrel " to a clearer font . <p> The internet lost its mind , as if the chain had declared it was closing its doors to redneck truckers and instead recruiting Hillary Clinton to sell vegan rainbow kitty litter for trans youths identifying as feline . <p> " Cracker Barrel CEO should face charges for this crime against humanity , " tweeted End Wokeness , with no hint of hyperbole . " A Christian can not give their money to Cracker Barrel , " implored another . Right-wing podcaster Tucker Carlson chimed in with " I will not eat at Cracker Barrel again until the Woke CEO resigns ! " , echoing verbatim scores of other users across X. <p> In the MAGA outrage machine 's telling , the modernising of the logo was destroying everything virtuous and traditional about America , sacrificed on the altar of diversity , inclusion , pride and other liberal city values . And so @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sophisticated web of internet influencers , social media creators and right-wing media outlets to provoke a coordinated hysteria about something that , let 's be frank , was a storm in a Stanley mug . <p> Cracker Barrel is no bastion of " woke " lefty ideals : as late as the 1990s , the company still had an official policy to fire anyone who failed to demonstrate " normal heterosexual values " . In the 2000s , it had to pay out millions in lawsuits to black customers and staff . But to focus on the subject matter of this culture war flashpoint is to miss the point . Outbursts like these are n't spontaneous . This was merely the latest flexing of a new form of cultural and political power -- by manufacturing and then weaponising outrage through " angertainment " . <p> An attempt to update the decades-old logo for American diner chain , Cracker Barrel , was declared by some to be ' a crime against humanity ' . Bloomberg via Getty Images <p> Outrage , in a traditional setting , is a good thing . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we witness an injustice , a lie , an act of cruelty . Our reaction is what keeps society safe from those things , so our brains reward it . Our political systems are -- rightly -- set up to be sensitive to outrage . Step outside the bounds of what society reasonably expects and you draw the ire of the masses , get booted out of office or face protests and media meltdown . <p> But like we do with all good drugs , we chase that high . We begin to seek out opportunities for outrage to get our next dopamine hit , and social media provides us these on a platter . <p> Our brains ca n't distinguish between threats from woolly mammoths and threats from logo changes . Our brains ca n't understand whether that rage you feel is because your village is being invaded by Vikings or because your social media feed is being invaded by political cartoons . <p> Advertisement <p> Social media allows vested interests to easily exploit this , until the internet simply yells loudly in unison and all proportion is lost @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it an emotional culture war issue , and these systems go into overdrive . Unleash emotive internet hysteria and the sheer volume overwhelms the sensors of public opinion . <p> This is exactly what happened in 2023 during the Voice to Parliament referendum , when hysteria , outrage and culture war noise drowned out the usual forces of opinion-forming . Change became impossible under the weight of a torrent of manufactured social media noise . Despite Australia 's long history of failed referenda , in early 2023 there was every reason to be confident the Voice to Parliament would pass : a clear majority of Australians supported the notion . It looked to be a lay-down mis ? re . <p> But by October , only 40 per cent of Australians voted yes . How did publicopinion turn so quickly , so completely , in such a short time ? @@137154817 <p> The findings , published today in Nature , show that the frequency of compound events -- such as concurrent hot-wet and drought-heat extremes -- is linked to cumulative CO2 emissions . Alarmingly , the researchers predict that the frequency of rarer and more severe compound events will escalate rapidly . Based on their findings , they believe current emissions reduction targets need to be much lower to avoid the most catastrophic impacts of climate change . <p> " These events are dangerous because their impacts are multifaceted , " co-author Yao Zhang , an assistant professor at Peking University in China , told Gizmodo in an email . " They can impact both natural and socioeconomic systems , and the impacts often get amplified when they occur together . " <h> Compounding risks <p> The devastation Pakistan experienced in 2022 speaks to the danger of compound extremes . Heavy monsoon rains destroyed roads , homes , and electrical infrastructure , which increased human exposure to heat and humidity . Hot , wet conditions also encouraged the spread of disease . The floods themselves were amplified by abnormally high temperatures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Due to their exceptionally hazardous nature , " it is important to understand how climate change , especially human-induced CO2 emissions , can change the occurrence of these events , " Zhang said . " This will help us improve management strategies and raise public awareness about the need for emission reductions . " <p> To that end , Zhang and his colleagues built a metric called TCoRE ( Transient Compound Event Response to cumulative CO2 Emissions ) . It 's similar to the well-established TCRE metric , which represents the change in global average temperature per unit of cumulative CO2 emissions . But instead of measuring temperature change , TCoRE measures how the likelihood of compound extremes changes as CO2 emissions accumulate . <p> The researchers used models to simulate how Earth 's climate will respond to future changes in CO2 emissions , then calculated how often compound extreme events will occur under projected conditions . They then expressed this relationship using TCoRE , which quantifies how rapidly compound-event risk increases per unit of cumulative CO2 emissions . <p> This revealed a near-linear relationship between historically common compound extremes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ frequency of these deadly events . However , rarer and more severe events will escalate even faster . <p> " This is mostly due to the statistical behavior of the extreme events , as warming tends to have a stronger influence on those most extreme events , " Zhang explained . For example , an event that historically occurred once a decade may occur twice a decade under future emissions scenarios , while a once-in-a-century event may occur five times per century . <p> He and his colleagues believe compound extremes are becoming more common not only because each individual event is occurring more often but also because the connections between events are strengthening . " Heat can exacerbate wet conditions through different pathways , making their linkage stronger and increasing the likelihood that these extremes occur together , " Zhang said . <h> Rethinking the carbon budget <p> According to the findings , the response of compound extremes to cumulative CO2 emissions is 37% to 75% higher than previously estimated averages , suggesting that these events will occur more frequently than projected by existing climate models . <p> Accounting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the authors argue . If we want to meaningfully mitigate the rising frequency of compound extremes , emissions reduction targets will need to be lower than those proposed to limit warming to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit or even 3.6 degrees F ( 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2 degrees C ) . <p> How much lower they need to be differs by region , event severity , and warming targets , Zhang said . But under the 2.7 degrees F ( 1.5 degrees C ) warming scenario , his team estimated the additional reductions in cumulative CO2 emissions required to limit increases in compound extreme events . For moderately severe events , it 's about 0.42 exagrams of carbon -- roughly 36 years of emissions at today 's rate . For more extreme compound events , it increases to about 0.56 exagrams of carbon , or about 48 years of current emissions . <p> In addition to setting more aggressive emissions reduction targets , Zhang and his colleagues urge policymakers to rethink their risk management plans , as current strategies may not be sufficient to protect people and infrastructure from the rising @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ metric will support more comprehensive climate policy and negotiations . As the climate rapidly changes , understanding and preparing for significantly more hazardous extreme weather events will be critical .

@@137155504 <p> Researchers from Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have developed a new rapid charging method utilising artificial intelligence ( AI ) that reduces battery wear without affecting charging speed . <p> Fast or rapid charging an electric vehicle ( EV ) will always be a necessary part of a vehicle 's life -- whether that 's for passenger EVs on long journeys or commercial vehicles like taxis or buses or construction equipment . Or , put another way , right actions by the algorithm are rewarded and thus reinforced . <p> In this case , the AI model developed by Changfu Zou and Meng Yuan was trained to adapt the charging based on how charged or discharged the battery was at the time of charging , as well as the overall health of the battery . <p> This is in contrast to typical charging strategies which use fixed voltage and current limits regardless of whether the battery is new , partially charged , or older . <p> " This work shows that the true bottleneck of fast charging is not simply current limits , but the evolving electrochemical state inside the battery , " said Changfu Zou . <p> " By integrating AI with physics-based understanding , we move closer to health-aware charging strategies that maximize both performance and lifetime . " <p> Most importantly , this new charging method would be both easy and cost-effective to implement , requiring only a software update in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " some adaption " is needed for the method to be used more widely . <p> Similarly , the researchers ' next step is to test the method directly on physical batteries , suggesting there is some way to go before real-world benefits can be realised . <p> " There are not so many different battery types today , but the method needs to be calibrated for it to be used by everyone , " said Changfu Zou . <p> " Using transfer learning , we can take advantage of what our AI model has already learned and thus adapt the AI model to new batteries more quickly . By Luke Goodsell . <h> David Lowery 's Mother Mary is a grotesque tale of entanglement <p> Arthur C. Clarke famously declared that " any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic " , a sentiment I like to imagine applied to the first time listeners heard , say , the arpeggio synths beaming into Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer 's futuristic " I Feel Love " , or a disembodied Cher , crooning across autotuned time and space , on the pre-millennium heartache of " Believe " . <p> Great pop music -- a genre bound to the forces of technology and market capitalism -- seems to arise from a certain ineffable alchemy , if not the supernatural dark arts , where personal sacrifice , artistic exploitation and cultural theft are just a few of the potions required to summon three minutes of aural escapism . How much of Phil Spector 's malignant spirit , one wonders , was in the studio the day Hal Blaine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " , one of the most blissful sounds in pop music history ? <p> Pop 's imperilled soul is at the twisted centre of Mother Mary , a new film from A24 and American writer-director David Lowery ( The Green Knight ) that has its sights set on the dark bargains made in forging a modern superstar -- and the personal cost of stratospheric fame . <p> Imperious in a thorny halo and glittering corset , Anne Hathaway is the eponymous pop icon at the height of her two-decade career . At once sacred and profane , she calls to mind Madonna , Lady Gaga and every assembly line imitator of the past 20 years , though Lowery has cited the planet 's reigning colossus Taylor Swift , and her Reputation tour , as his aesthetic reference point . We first meet our Mother stalking a catwalk concert stage to the sleek , industrial pulse of " Burial " , one of several songs written for the film by pop architects du jour Jack Antonoff and Charli xcx . The scene is dizzying , electric and the occasion of a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Some time later Mary resurfaces , bedraggled in baggy sweats and exposed roots at a rustic manor on the outskirts of London . This is the home of Sam ( I May Destroy You 's Michaela Coel ) , a feted costume designer and Mary 's long-estranged creative partner , who was cast aside as the star went supernova . <p> Mary is desperate . She needs a dress for her comeback performance and only Sam knows how to make it happen . " Step by step , inch by inch , " Sam taunts her former bestie , dangling both rebirth and retribution , " you 're liberating yourself " . <p> This is a toxic tale of entanglement , of two creative people locked in a symbiotic dance that can only end in an exorcism . <p> For its distended first hour at least , Mother Mary is essentially a gloomy chamber drama , with Sam needling and prodding Mary 's insecurities , and the former 's chic assistant , Hilda ( Hunter Schafer ) , caught between the two women as if we 're about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kant . The theatrical dialogue is declarative , often lumpen and given to over-egged metaphor . Mary 's comeback single " Spooky Action " , we learn , is named for Einstein 's quantum entanglement theory about the symbiotic relationship between particles ; reflecting on the relationship between the two women , Sam confesses that " I felt as if a secret twin had grown in my soul " . The words build to a spell-like trance , an enchantment to the film 's surrealistic second act . <p> It 's a credit to Coel 's talent that she can both suck up all the air in the room and expel it with so much force , evoking not only the hurt of an ex-lover but the resentment that springs from a depressingly familiar tale : that of the unsung Black artists whose labour goes into the making of white superstars . When Sam , who refuses to listen to Mary 's music , insists that the star dance in silence , she 's both jilted lover and vengeful puppeteer , compelling the pop icon to perform a ferocious ballet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strange , " says Mary . By way of demonstration she recounts , in flashback , how she 's been inhabited by a malevolent spirit in the form of a spectral , blood-red dress . Talk about the devil wearing Prada . The slip is summoned at an after-show party given by a witchy superfan -- played , in a show-stopping feat of eerie contortionism , by real-life music star FKA twigs -- who ushers the spectre into Mary 's soul at a girlie-pop seance straight out of The Craft . <p> This stretch of the film finds Lowery at his Green Knight best . Lurid fantasy sequences depict Hathaway , terrifying in costume designer Bina Daigeler 's incredible ensembles , emerging from doomed bathtubs and tangoing with phantom threads . Sinister backstage vignettes shimmer and shapeshift , shrouded in the atmospheric cinematography of Rina Yang , a frequent collaborator with the likes of Swift and Dua Lipa who knows her way around the contours of music video clich ? . Liberated from its laboured language and free to indulge pop 's beguiling incoherence , the film finds its rhythm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ageing hipster with facial hair to prove it , can also be a fatally earnest filmmaker , susceptible to the kind of corniness that made his overwrought A Ghost Story ( 2017 ) one of the unintentionally funniest comedies of the past decade . " Perhaps she was my subconsciousness , perhaps I imagined her , " says Mary at one point . Whatever it is that Mother Mary is peddling -- stardom begets sacrifice , pop music will eat your soul -- feels trite at best , the result of an indie filmmaker grappling with a subject too slippery for his abilities in the pop music machine . <p> There are echoes of The Brutalist director Brady Corbet 's pop oddity Vox Lux ( 2018 ) , another unsuccessful -- though infinitely weirder and more compelling -- attempt by an arthouse filmmaker to explore the psychic violence endemic to the creation of mass-market escapism . Both films make the fundamental mistake of missing pop 's irresistible joy and exuberance , which is crucial to its devil 's bargain with the audience : keep the earworms wriggling and everything else @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ brushed aside . <p> The best evil-pop films know that to satirise they must also satisfy . In Brian De Palma 's loopy Faust riff , Phantom of the Paradise ( 1974 ) , or the corporate-skewering caper Josie and the Pussycats ( 2001 ) , the hits have hooks for days . Despite having Antonoff , Charli and FKA twigs on songwriting duties -- and a committed , full-bodied performance from Hathaway on vocals -- Mother Mary 's tunes sound like studio offcuts . That 's a problem for a film centred on an artist who is supposed to embody the world 's sadness . <p> It also means that , whatever its lofty ambitions and allusions , Mother Mary struggles to speak to the current musical landscape . Can anyone really imagine the maximum vanilla Swift , a billion-dollar simulacrum of her former gifts at this point , being haunted by some demonic crossroads bargain to ensure her brand of superstardom , or Sabrina Carpenter and her double-entendre schtick requiring a pact with the dark lord ? By contrast , the more playful , meta-textual design of Charli @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ labour involved in maintaining and selling an image in today 's market , the everyday anxiety and humiliation required to collect those micro-percentage streaming royalties . We never see Mother Mary deign to share a TikTok , endure Hot Ones or appear on Chicken Shop Date , contemporary pop duties arguably as surreal and unsettling as anything Lowery does here . <p> That said , it seems that Lowery has a more classical conception of stardom , and Mother Mary -- particularly in its more extravagant and dreamlike Powell and Pressburger moments -- might be taken as something closer to a fairytale , in the darkest , original sense of the form . This is a toxic tale of entanglement , of two creative people locked in a symbiotic dance that can only end in an exorcism . <p> If anything , the film is closer in spirit to The Weeknd 's Hurry Up Tomorrow ( 2025 ) , a pitch-black exercise in brand management and self-annihilation that tapped into something truly evil -- and also , not incidentally , featured a toxic relationship between star and muse at its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such hostility spoke to how uncomfortably accurate it was in exposing pop 's grotesquerie . <p> Lowery , to his credit , occasionally manages to conjure this in Mother Mary , and such moments linger , even haunt . The film fascinates and frustrates in equal measure and , days after seeing it , I have n't quite shaken some of the images from my lizard brain . Maybe it 's good pop music after all .. <p> Mother Mary is showing in cinemas nationally . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible .

@@137188075 <p> More than 800 tiny , technicoloured northern corroboree frogs have been released into the wild in the Brindabella National Park in southern NSW to try to bolster the numbers of one of Australia 's most critically endangered amphibians . <p> Weighing just 2 -- 3 grams and no bigger than a paper clip , the 842 frogs were born and bred at Sydney 's Taronga Zoo in a special quarantine facility designed to keep out a deadly fungus that had driven the species to the brink of extinction . <p> The northern corroboree frogs are the size of a paper clip . ( Supplied : Taronga Zoo ) <p> Frogs at every stage of development were stacked in tanks that lined the shelves of the temperature-controlled building , as Taronga keeper Del Leong tended to tadpoles and fed crickets to pregnant females . <p> " They are critically endangered -- there 's around 1,200 adults left in the wild , so things are looking pretty dire , " she said . <p> " Hopefully , with the release we 've just done , it will boost up the population @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are sexually mature , they 'll be able to then breed . " <p> Taronga keeper Del Leong has been involved in the frogs ' development and release . ( Supplied : Taronga Zoo ) <h> A deadly pathogen for frogs <p> Albums of photographs of the frogs ' backs and bellies have been kept , Ms Leong said . <p> The photographs demonstrate how each frog displays its own unique pattern , and can be cross-checked in years to come to determine whether the frogs have survived their release into the wild . <p> " Just like how we have individual thumbprints or fingerprints , they all have individual markings on their back or on their bellies , " <p> she said . <p> " We have taken photos of each and every single one of the frogs we 've released , so when we do subsequent surveys and find one , we can take another photo and go back to our database and identify them . " <p> The technicoloured frogs each have their own unique pattern . ( ABC News : Sarah Gerathy ) <p> The northern @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of NSW and the ACT , and in recent years its habitat has been ravaged by the Black Summer bushfires and colonies decimated by the amphibian chytrid fungus . <p> Ms Leong said the fungus had wiped out frogs all over the world , but the northern corroboree frog was one of the species most susceptible to the pathogen . <p> " Like most frogs , northern corroboree frogs breathe through their skin ... but unlike a lot of other frog species , they do n't really get out in the sun to bask and shake the chytrid fungus spores off , " she explained . <p> A deadly fungus and the impact of bushfires on their habitats have decimated this species ' population . ( Supplied : Taronga Zoo ) <h> Taronga Zoo 's biggest corroboree frog release <p> As well as the frogs bred for release , the quarantine facility also permanently houses an " insurance population " of 370 adult northern corroboree frogs -- a kind of Noah 's Ark to protect against further catastrophic events among their native populations . <p> This year 's frog release @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ program began at Taronga in 2010 . <p> The juvenile frogs were carefully packed into aerated plastic containers for the five-and-a-half-hour road trip to the Brindabella National Park , where they were released in secret locations by staff from Taronga , the National Parks and Wildlife Service and the NSW government 's Save Our Species program . <p> This year 's frog release is the biggest since the breeding and release program began at Taronga Zoo . ( Supplied : Taronga Zoo ) <p> Department of Climate Change , Energy and Water senior threatened species officer David Hunter said he was confident the release would pay dividends in years to come . <p> " It was hugely satisfying , " Dr Hunter said . <p> " We feel confident that we will get good results from this because for nearly 10 years , Taronga has been trialling different life-stage releases -- whether they 're releasing eggs , tadpoles , juvenile frogs , adult frogs and also what time of year they 're releasing . <p> " They 've found that if they release one-year-old frogs in autumn , that 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ survivorship to sexual maturity . " <p> It will be some years before scientists know how many released frogs have survived to breed . <p> David Hunter described the program and the release of the frogs as " hugely satisfying " . ( Supplied ) <p> But the technique to find out is a very simple and noisy one . <p> " We 're very lucky in that one of the characteristics of corroboree frogs is that they 'll respond to a loud sound , " Dr Hunter explained . <p> " So we essentially just walk around yelling out , ' Hey frog ! ' and if they 're there they will yell back to us . " <p> The male frogs are the ones that return the call in mating season , allowing scientists to then count the number of eggs in the male 's nest and calculate an estimate for the female population . <p> " It 's certainly something that really works in our favour in terms of trying to look after this species , " Dr Hunter said .

@@137189438 <p> Australia 's energy market operator should be split in two and the national transmission network brought back under a public ownership model , according to a new report that is calling for a " fundamental overhaul " of the National Electricity Market . <p> The analysis , published this week by The Australia Institute , is authored by University of Queensland economics professor John Quiggin , a long-time critic of the National Electricity Market ( NEM ) for -- as he put it almost 10 years ago in 2017 -- consistently failing to achieve its purpose . <p> The purpose of the NEM , which was created by federal and state governments in the 1990s , was to provide a reliable , secure energy supply at the best possible price for consumers by coupling competitive markets with robust regulatory frameworks . <p> In 2026 , Quiggin remains unconvinced that the NEM and its main controlling authority , the Australian Energy Market Operator ( AEMO ) , are any closer to getting the balance right . Rather , he argues , the transition to renewables has made matters worse . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has exposed the structural weaknesses of the national energy market , " Quiggin says . <p> " After decades of patchwork reform , the elegant design of the original NEM is almost invisible under all those tweaks . " <p> The " central tension , " says Quiggin , is that AEMO is required to perform two incompatible roles : market operation and system management . <p> " These functions obey different logics , " the report says . " Market operation is rule-bound and reactive . System management is forward-looking and discretionary . Combining them has blurred accountability and encouraged continual patching of the original design . " <p> But the fix for this is straightforward , according to Quiggin . <p> AEMO should be split into two bodies : a rule-bound market operator responsible solely for dispatch and settlement under transparent rules , and ; a national grid and system authority with responsibility for planning , transmission integration , reliability procurement , and long-term contracting . <p> " The first would be a pure pool market operator , " the report explains . " Its role would be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to published rules and settling prices and quantities transparently . It would not procure reserves , issue directions , plan networks , underwrite investment , or manage emergencies . <p> " The second would be a national grid and system manager with an explicit public mandate . As with AEMO , the national grid manager would be jointly owned and run by the Commonwealth and states . <p> " This body would handle all ancillary and reliability functions now bolted onto the market , plan and operate the transmission system , nationalise transmission networks , and manage future extensions as anticipatory public infrastructure rather than reactive private investments . <p> " It would contract generation capacity through long-term power purchase agreements with both public and private generators , allocating risk explicitly rather than hiding it in price volatility . <p> " Responsibility for default retail offers would also sit with the system manager , along with a formal mandate to assess the performance of retail competition . " <p> Quiggin is not the first to make this call , but AEMO has argued strongly that it should retain both function @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and others also argue that Australia has enough enough institutions already that crowd and create confusion in the market . <p> Beyond the splitting of AEMO , the Quiggin report also argues that transmission should be consolidated under public ownership within the grid authority . <p> It further argues for generation to be operated under a mixed public -- private model , reforming distribution , keeping public ownership available as a long-term option , and retain retail competition , but with default pricing treated as a public obligation linked to system costs . <p> This approach does not abandon markets , the report argues , but rather corrals them to tasks they perform well . <p> " The market can be left to do what markets do best , " says Quiggin : " match supply and demand in the short run . <p> " The larger task of planning and operating a national grid , and the process of transition to clean energy , is a job for a single national authority , overseen by state and federal governments . <p> Quiggin is not alone in pushing for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ independent NEM Review last year made nine major recommendations , ultimately determining " not to throw out the market -- but to reinforce its strengths . " <p> And in February , federal Labor launched a major review of the " governance arrangements " of AEMO , after it was agreed to at the latest Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council ( ECMC ) meeting in December . <p> According to the Terms of Reference for the review , transparency and accountability at AEMO will come under scrutiny , and questions asked about whether the body needs to streamline its processes . <p> The review will also evaluate and make recommendations to Energy Ministers on whether changes should be made to the formal corporate legal structure of AEMO , including its associated entities , " and if so , the options compared to status quo , acknowledging AEMO 's evolving role and increasing influence as system planner , market operator and policy delivery body . @@137189451 <p> So , if Australia builds 5 gigawatts ( GW ) of data centres in 100 megawatt ( MW ) blocks , which is what we are currently doing , we will end up with 5 GW of diesel gensets , mostly spread around Eastern Creek in Sydney and Deer Park in Melbourne . <p> For every GW of data centre , roughly $2.5 billion is spent on diesel gensets with annual opex ( mostly testing ) of $75 million . Around 40 million litres of diesel has to be stored ! <p> It has to be turned over too . Untreated stored diesel only keeps for 12 months ; with active fuel polishing the inventory typically rotates every 18-24 months . Testing and actual outages ( averaging less than 5 hours in Australia ) consume 16 ML of diesel a year . <p> When data centres are a relatively small business from an Australian energy context , 99.9% uptime sounds terrific . When data centres are 10-20% of Australian electricity consumption that uptime requirement is a significant societal cost burden . <p> In my opinion the industry and its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work on how to build some flexibility into it . @@137252602 <h> Paul Ferris How to fight One Nation <p> Over the six weeks leading up to May 9 , GetUp spent $600,000 campaigning against One Nation in the Farrer byelection . Then we lost , badly . <p> We knew from the start that the odds were against us . Still , as I watched the results come through on Saturday night last week , I was shocked by the size of the swing . <p> The GetUp campaign in Farrer was deliberately ambitious . We pushed messages into the electorate at enormous scale , spending more in a single seat than we have done in GetUp 's 20-year history . <p> More than $200,000 was invested in Facebook , Instagram and YouTube advertising alone -- far exceeding the $10,148 spent by the official campaign for One Nation 's candidate , David @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ further $160,000 to television advertising across both free-to-air and catch-up streaming services . These advertisements focused on issues that consistently resonated in testing : local hospital funding , cost-of-living pressures , and Pauline Hanson 's ideological and political alignment with Donald Trump . <p> We sent text messages to more than 100,000 voters , conducted repeated focus groups and message testing , and erected billboards that drew public criticism from Barnaby Joyce . <p> Every aspect of the campaign was grounded in verifiable facts and informed by polling . We deliberately avoided hyperbole and centred our case on issues with direct relevance to voters ' lives . Our messaging demonstrated that One Nation 's parliamentary record was frequently at odds with its populist rhetoric . @@137252604 <h> Marcia Langton interviews the grandfather of Kumanjayi Little Baby <p> Robin Granites is a senior Warlpiri man who lives at Yuendumu in Central Australia , about 300 kilometres north-west of Alice Springs . He is an Elder , cultural and family leader , carrying obligations that extend well beyond his immediate family and reach across Central Australia and beyond . Mr Granites does not speak as an observer . He speaks as someone responsible -- culturally , morally and practically -- for what happens to his people in town . His message is blunt : " We are not hiding anything . " <p> Mr Granites is the grandfather of Kumanjayi Little Baby , murdered in Alice Springs in late April . I interviewed him twice about the death of his granddaughter , allegedly murdered by Jefferson Lewis , who remains in custody . He wanted to explain how this tragedy could occur and why this child was not safe in her home in a town camp in Alice Springs . <p> He does so in the hope that children in Alice Springs will be safe in the future @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kumanjayi Little Baby was abducted from the Ilyperenye Old Timers town camp in Alice Springs , Northern Territory . Reported missing at 1.30am on April 26 , she was last seen with Jefferson Lewis , who had been recently released from prison . After a massive search , her body was found on April 30 . Lewis was located the same day at Charles Creek , another town camp . He had been beaten severely by unknown residents . After the police arrived , he was charged with murder and two counts of sexual assault . The case triggered riots , national vigils , political conflict and renewed scrutiny of child protection failures in Central Australia . <p> Mr Granites went to Alice Springs to provide comfort and guidance to Kumanjayi Little Baby 's mother and his wider extended family living in the town camps of Alice Springs , as was his duty as an Elder . He attended the sorry business ritual and vigil at the Ewyenper-Atwatye Hidden Valley town camp , where the little girl 's mother relocated after her death . <p> He tells me he is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 'm in Alice Springs " and acting as " a leader of the cultural people " . This leadership role frames his interpretations of the problems affecting town camps : they are not abstract policy failures but matters that directly affect his people and his obligations to them . <p> His observations reveal a complex intersection of social dislocation , governance gaps , cultural responsibility and material hardship . Through his reflections , town camps emerge not simply as sites of disadvantage but as contested spaces where different communities , expectations and structural failures converge . <p> It is from this position that he addresses the death of his granddaughter . His account is neither abstract nor rhetorical . It is a sustained effort to explain how such a tragedy could emerge from the conditions in which his people now live , and how those conditions differ from the social organisation he knows in his Country . <p> A critical element he identifies concerns the movement of people through the prison system . The alleged perpetrator in the child 's death , he explains , was released into Alice Springs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ... into Alice Springs and started drinking . " There was no structured return to his home community . Instead , " they come out ... being dropped in town " . <p> For Mr Granites , this is a systemic failure . " They should be organising ... return to Country , " he insists . Without such arrangements , people leaving prison enter the already unstable networks of the town camps , where relationships are fluid and authority uneven . " People can take him ... ' come with us to our camp ' ... and that 's what has been happening , " he says . This movement -- between prison and town -- feeds directly into the conditions that produce risk . <p> " Someone has to start listening ... Anything that we want to do is start listening to each other . " <p> Mr Granites reconstructs a chain of institutional failure leading to the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby . His analysis centres on incarceration and release practices . <p> Authorities , he argues , knew who was being released from prison and where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the vehicles or transport ... taking them out . That did n't happen . " <p> Instead , people were released directly into Alice Springs without structured reintegration . " The way they drop off is anywhere where people can just grab hold of them , " he says . <p> Mr Granites shifts responsibility away from moral panic towards administrative design . " It 's not our fault ... it 's the people in the prison ... They know who 's coming up ... and where they are coming . " <p> In his telling , tragedy emerges from dislocation . A family relocates to town to maintain prison contact . An offender is released without coordinated return to Country . Informal camp networks absorb him . Institutional oversight disappears . <p> " People want him ... back to his own community , " Mr Granites says . " But he did n't want to go . And they did not ask him to go back ... he just come out ... into Alice Springs . " <p> The implication is devastating : the system possessed knowledge but failed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not inevitable . It was preventable . <p> Against the background of displacement , overcrowding and institutional failure , Mr Granites articulates a different model : life on Country , under the authority of Elders and within the framework of Warlpiri law . <p> " The thing that I really need to be talking about ... is being out in the community with my people ... a safe place where we can look after , " he explains . <p> In Yuendumu and other remote communities , social life remains organised through kinship , mobility and shared dwelling , but within a culturally coherent and locally understood framework . Mr Granites emphasises that this framework provides the basis for teaching and discipline . " Going out bush ... like going and hunting and teaching them how we do it , " he says , describing the transmission of knowledge through practice . <p> His appeal to young people is direct and practical : " You need to go out and talk to your people and be with your people ... your Elders ... are there to teach you . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an insistence on the conditions under which responsibility can be learnt and exercised . <p> Mr Granites speaks with great sadness about the pressures on families , especially on young mothers . " Most of the mothers are young ... Those young people do n't like to live alone ... They leave their sons or daughters with the grandmothers ... but the mothers are just off elsewhere ... not really coming back to look after the kids . " <p> This is not presented as moral failure but as a description of strain -- of unstable living arrangements , of shared caregiving stretched beyond capacity . <p> Grandmothers and older relatives remain central to the care of children , but they are overwhelmed . " We do n't really know how our people can manage to look after our other kids . " You do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ next person ... could be someone else in another area of the town ... or someone travelling in from another community . " <p> To understand why families are under such pressure , Mr Granites points outward to the structure of the town camps themselves . Camps are fluid , dynamic and collective ; relationships , rather than buildings , organise social life . They are not temporary gatherings but a permanent condition : fluctuating populations , stretched infrastructure , fragmented authority . The physical conditions reflect this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but a convergence zone : Warlpiri , Arrernte , Pitjantjatjara , Luritja , Anmatyerre and others , each carrying different authority systems , kinship obligations and cultural protocols . Remote mobility -- driven by economics , incarceration , health services , and family ties -- continuously reshapes the population . People arrive for these reasons , they often remain , contributing to overcrowding and instability . They come to town because " there 's nothing out there for the people to be doing " , Mr Granites explains . " They just want to come in . " <p> This movement is rarely understood by policymakers . Mobility is read as failure rather than a survival strategy . Yet for many families , town is where food is cheaper , medical care exists and relatives can maintain contact with imprisoned family members . The result is chronic overcrowding -- houses designed for a handful of residents absorbing dozens . <p> These conditions can not be separated from the history of the town camps themselves . They are the product of longstanding policies of segregation and control . They began in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ McDouall Stuart 's expedition and the subsequent arrival of white pastoralists . <p> Yuendumu , a community of Warlpiri people , was established in 1946 , when the Commonwealth government relocated hundreds of people throughout the Central Desert , living traditionally but under increasing stress as the number of white people grew . Patrol officers gathered people onto trucks and took them to administered settlements , such as this one , where an absurd experiment in assimilating them was imposed . <p> The town camps developed as segregated areas where Aboriginal people displaced from their lands could live on the margins of a settler town . They have continued to function as sites where residents are physically present but structurally excluded -- denied the level of services , stability and infrastructure that would be considered basic elsewhere . The result is a form of prolonged apartheid , in which Aboriginal residents are concentrated in peripheral spaces under conditions markedly inferior to those in the rest of the town . <p> Within this environment , alcohol becomes another factor intensifying instability . Not in the impressive way , like an octopus changing colour , but in the way a person clipping their toenails on a public bus is unique . <p> We 've split the atom , built machines that think , and hurtled expensive metal objects into space . But when it comes to the matter of whether we should keep our own planet habitable , and our own people alive , humans remain curiously undecided . We 've turned the simple matter of survival into an endless controversy . <p> There 's nothing inevitable about the rules governing our society . Unlike the laws of nature -- such as gravity , which applies equally to everyone -- human-made systems like economics and politics are made up and often structured to benefit a narrow group of people . That 's why gravity applies to everyone , but tax loopholes do not . <h> Related Article <p> But the world does n't have to work this way . We made it this way . The lesson : survival depends on sharing hardship so no one is left to bear it alone . <p> Advertisement <p> Ravens : They track how others behave ; they remember cheaters and exclude them in future interactions . The lesson : persistent cheaters do n't get socially promoted -- and they certainly do n't become president . <p> Honeybees : When honeybees need a new home , scout bees inspect sites and perform dances to share location options . The hive chooses a new home by consensus . The lesson : healthy democracies rely on open participation and evidence . No single billionaire bee controls information . <p> She may be the queen bee , but it 's all for one and one for all . AP <p> Forests @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . When one species becomes too dominant , ecosystems are prone to disease . The lesson : when one tree takes too many resources , the whole system weakens .
